title: Appendix — Additional Technical Notes
text: This appendix gathers standalone technical notes that do not fit cleanly into the geo-data or model/metric appendices —derivations, tricks and implementation details of the codebase that are worth writing down once, in one place.

title: Appendix — Additional Technical Notes
text:
Large-Scale Cosine Similarity Statistics (group_cosine_stats)
Chapter 2 already defined the cosine similarity between two vectors and used it, repeatedly, to answer a within-group question: given all the embedding vectors covering a single geometry, say every AlphaEarth pixel inside a CVEGEO, a street, or an AGEB, how similar are they to each other? That is exactly the “Benchmark computation” behind the CVEGEO/MZA/AGEB similarity heatmaps of Chapter 2, and it is what group_cosine_stats from src/utils/similarity.py computes: the mean, median and standard deviation of every pairwise cosine similarity within a group of \(n\) vectors.
The obvious way to get there, computing the full \(n\times n\) similarity matrix and reading its upper triangle, costs \(O(n^2 d)\) in time and \(O(n^2)\) in memory, for \(d\)-dimensional vectors. That is fine for a handful of points, but it is infeasible once a group has hundreds of thousands of pixels, which is the normal case at a \(10\text{m}\) resolution over a whole municipality. group_cosine_stats avoids materializing that matrix entirely for the mean and the standard deviation, and only falls back to it, in bounded chunks, when strictly necessary for the median.

Setup
Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) be the set of the \(n\) embedding vectors as rows (here \(d=64\) for AlphaEarth). By normalizing each row to unit length,
\[ U_i = \frac{X_i}{\lVert X_i \rVert_2} \]
the cosine similarity between any two rows becomes a simple dot product, \(s_{ij} = U_i \cdot U_j\), exactly the definition already given in Chapter 2. Zero-norm rows are left at the origin instead of generating a division by zero, the sensible convention for a “no signal” vector —although it is worth noting that such a row is then not really a unit vector (\(\lVert U_i \rVert = 0\), not \(1\)), so its self-similarity \(s_{ii}\) is \(0\) instead of \(1\); the identities below assume that every row is a genuine unit vector, and are therefore exact whenever the group has no all-zero rows, and only slightly approximate (by a fraction of a pair, for each zero row) otherwise. The function returns the mean, median and standard deviation of \(\{s_{ij} : i<j\}\), the \(\binom{n}{2}\) pairwise similarities between the \(n\) rows.


The exact mean, via a Gram trace identity
The mean does not require any pairwise similarity to be computed directly. Let \(S = \sum_{i=1}^{n} U_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\) be the (vector) sum of all the normalized rows. Expanding its squared norm:
\[ \lVert S \rVert^2 = S \cdot S = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n U_i \cdot U_j = \sum_{i=1}^n \underbrace{\lVert U_i \rVert^2}_{=\,1} \; + \sum_{i \neq j} U_i \cdot U_j = n + 2\sum_{i<j} s_{ij}\]
using that each \(U_i\) is a unit vector, and that each unordered pair \(i<j\) is counted twice in the \(i \neq j\) sum (once as \((i,j)\), once as \((j,i)\), with \(s_{ij}=s_{ji}\)). Solving for the pairwise sum:
\[ \sum_{i<j} s_{ij} = \frac{\lVert S \rVert^2 - n}{2} \]
which is exactly sum_s = (S @ S - n) / 2.0 in the code. Computing \(S\) costs \(O(nd)\) (a single pass over the data), and \(\lVert S \rVert^2\) is then a single \(O(d)\) dot product —the \(\binom{n}{2}\) pairwise terms never have to be formed individually. The mean is this sum divided by the number of pairs \(\binom{n}{2}\).


The exact variance, via the Gram matrix in feature space
The same trick extends to the second moment, \(\sum_{i<j} s_{ij}^2\), needed for the variance, but it uses a different matrix: the \(d \times d\) Gram matrix over features, \(G = U^{\top}U\), not the \(n\times n\) matrix of pairwise similarities \(UU^{\top}\) (whose entries are the \(s_{ij}\), but which is exactly the object we are trying to avoid building). Expanding the squared Frobenius norm of \(G\):
\[ \lVert G \rVert_F^2 = \sum_{a,b=1}^{d} G_{ab}^2 = \sum_{a,b}\left(\sum_i U_{ia}U_{ib}\right)\left(\sum_j U_{ja}U_{jb}\right) = \sum_{i,j}\left(\sum_a U_{ia}U_{ja}\right)\left(\sum_b U_{ib}U_{jb}\right) = \sum_{i,j} s_{ij}^2 \]
so summing the squared entries of the small \(d\times d\) matrix \(G\) gives us, for free, the sum of \(s_{ij}^2\) over every ordered pair \((i,j)\), including \(i=j\) (where \(s_{ii}=1\)). Separating that diagonal exactly as before:
\[ \sum_{i,j} s_{ij}^2 = n + 2\sum_{i<j} s_{ij}^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sum_{i<j} s_{ij}^2 = \frac{\lVert G \rVert_F^2 - n}{2} \]
which is sum_s2 = (np.sum(G * G) - n) / 2.0. The variance then follows from the usual identity \(\mathrm{Var}(s) = \mathbb{E}[s^2] - \mathbb{E}[s]^2\), clipped at zero to absorb floating-point rounding. Forming \(G=U^{\top}U\) costs \(O(nd^2)\); since \(d=64\) is fixed and small, this is linear in \(n\) in all practical terms, against the \(O(n^2 d)\) of the naive approach —the difference between a computation that runs in milliseconds and one that never finishes.


The median: no closed form, so exact-if-cheap, sampled otherwise
Order statistics such as the median have no equivalent algebraic shortcut; there is no way to recover “the middle value” from a handful of summary sums the way the mean and the variance were recovered above. group_cosine_stats therefore branches on how many pairs there are:

Exact, chunked, when \(\binom{n}{2} \le\) max_exact_pairs (5,000,000 by default): the upper triangle of the similarity matrix is still built, but row block by row block (chunk rows, 4096 by default), so that peak memory is bounded by chunk \(\times\, n\) instead of the full \(n\times n\). Each pair is visited exactly once and the true median is returned.
Sampled, above that threshold: sample_size random index pairs \((i,j)\) are drawn uniformly (with replacement) from \(\{1,\dots,n\}^2\), self-pairs are discarded, and their similarities are computed directly as row-wise dot products. The median of this random sample is reported as an estimate of the population median —a standard consequence of the fact that sample quantiles converge to the true population quantile as the sample grows, the same law-of-large-numbers argument that justifies using a sample mean in the first place. In the (extremely unlikely) case that every draw lands on a self-pair, the exact mean is returned instead, since, for a strongly concentrated similarity distribution, the mean is already a reasonable substitute.

Naive

\(O(n^2 d)\)
\(O(nd)\)

\(O(n^2 d)\)

title: Appendix — Geospatial Data Structures and Operations
text: This appendix gathers, in a single place, the geospatial concepts, formats and operations actually used throughout this repository. It is not a general GIS reference, just a quick map back to the ideas and code paths this project depends on, for anyone who needs a refresher while reading the previous chapters.
crumbs: Appendix — Geospatial Data Structures and Operations

title: Appendix — Geospatial Data Structures and Operations
text:
Geospatial Data Structures

Vector data: points, lines and polygons
Vector data represents discrete geometric objects with exact coordinates: Point, LineString (and MultiLineString), and Polygon (and MultiPolygon). Most of what this repository handles is vector data:

Crime incidents are Points, built from raw lat/lon columns with gpd.points_from_xy.
Streets are LineStrings (09e.shp), later split corner to corner into shorter segments.
Municipalities, AGEBs and the CDMX boundary are Polygons (09m.shp, 09a.shp, 09ent.shp).



Raster data (pixel grid)
Raster data represents a phenomenon as a regular grid of cells (pixels), each with one or more band values, instead of discrete geometric objects. AlphaEarth embeddings are natively distributed in this form —a vector of 64 values per 10m pixel, as multiband GeoTIFFs. src/etl/process_embeddings.py is what converts that raster into the tabular rows (lon, lat, A00..A63) the rest of the pipeline works with.



General raster data structure




File formats used in this repository

Shapefile (.shp, plus its companion files .shx/.dbf/.prj) — the classic multi-file vector format; used for each INEGI political division layer under data/spatial/pd/.
GeoParquet — parquet files with a geometry column, read and written with geopandas.read_parquet / to_parquet; used for the training sets and the processed AlphaEarth pixel tables, since it keeps geometry, embeddings and attributes in a single columnar file, suitable for partitioning.
GeoJSON — a text/JSON vector format; the output of the point-to-geometry aggregation step (src/etl/assign_point_to_geometry.py, driver="GeoJSON").
Flat CSV/parquet with lat/lon columns — not really a geometry format, just two floating-point columns promoted to Point geometries on demand with gpd.points_from_xy whenever a spatial operation is actually needed.



H3: global discrete grid
H3 divides the globe into hexagonal cells at multiple resolutions, each with a unique cell id —a discrete alternative to a raw lat/lon grid. h3_heatmap from src/eda/core.py uses it (h3.latlng_to_cell, h3.cell_to_latlng) to group crime points into hexagonal cells for a density heatmap, which reads better than a raw point cloud once the number of points grows.



Uber’s H3 geo-indexing (From: https://www.uber.com/gb/en/blog/h3/)

title: Appendix — Geospatial Data Structures and Operations
text:
Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)
Def (CRS): a Coordinate Reference System defines how the numerical coordinates of a geometry map to real positions on Earth —its datum, its projection (if it has one) and its units.



Geometric foundation of the CRS



Geographic CRS (e.g. EPSG:4326 / WGS84) — coordinates are (longitude, latitude) in degrees. Convenient for storage and for global data, but a degree is not a constant unit of distance (a degree of longitude shrinks toward the poles), so it is the wrong CRS for distance, area or buffer computations.
Projected CRS (e.g. EPSG:6372, EPSG:3857) — coordinates are in a flat unit, usually meters, obtained by projecting the curved Earth onto a flat surface. Correct for distance-based work, at the cost of some distortion that grows with the area covered.

CRSs actually used in this repository:

EPSG:4326 — the native/storage CRS for the crime incident points, the AlphaEarth embeddings, and most of the raw shapefiles.
EPSG:6372 (Mexico ITRF2008 / LCC, meters) — used to reproject the crime points before DBSCAN clustering (src/eda/core.py), since DBSCAN’s eps is a real distance and only makes sense in meters, not degrees.
EPSG:3857 (Web Mercator) — used to reproject the street network and the CDMX boundary before drawing a CartoDB basemap with contextily (src/visuals/flash_highlight_showcase.py), since web tiles are always served in this projection.

Reprojecting a GeoDataFrame is a single call:
gdf_3857 = gdf.to_crs(3857)
A recurring source of bugs in this kind of project is combining two layers that are in different CRSs, or measuring distance/area in a geographic one —always check gdf.crs before joining, buffering or plotting a basemap under two layers.

title: Appendix — Geospatial Data Structures and Operations
text:
Fundamental Spatial Operations

Points from coordinates
gpd.GeoDataFrame(df, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(df["lon"], df["lat"]), crs="EPSG:4326")
Used everywhere a CSV or parquet only brings lat/lon columns instead of a real geometry column (src/etl/assign_point_to_geometry.py, src/etl/get_training_sets.py).


Spatial join (sjoin) and nearest-neighbor join (sjoin_nearest)
Def: a spatial join attaches attributes from one layer to another based on a spatial predicate (intersects, contains, nearest, …) instead of a shared key column.

sjoin(..., predicate="intersects") — assigns the crime points to the AGEB polygon within which they fall (agg_points_to_geometry, POLYGON branch).
sjoin_nearest(...) — assigns each crime point to its nearest street segment instead of requiring it to fall exactly on the line (agg_points_to_geometry, LINESTRING branch); it is also used to attach the AlphaEarth pixels and the MZA socio-demographic centroids to the street geometries.



Buffering
.buffer(distance) expands a geometry outward by distance (in the units of the layer’s own CRS), turning a line or a point into a polygon. It is used to convert a street LINESTRING into a corridor-like polygon, so that it can be treated as an area for pixel coverage aggregation (src/etl/assign_point_to_geometry.py).



Example from Shapely’s official page




Centroid
.centroid returns the central point of a geometry. It is used to convert the MZA (block) polygons into unique representative points before joining them to the streets (src/etl/get_socioecon_data.py), and to place a single marker for a street segment in the animated demos (src/visuals/flash_highlight_showcase.py).



Example of a centroid (By Satyakamk. Original png by B Axelrod - Originally a png with the same name., Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=2527898)




Splitting geometries

At intersections — split_streets_at_intersections from src/utils/geom.py walks each street line, uses a spatial index to find nearby candidate lines, computes their exact intersection points, and cuts the line at each of them with shapely.ops.split. This is how the raw street network becomes the corner-to-corner segments used as the spatial unit throughout the whole crime modeling pipeline.
By length — split_gdf_by_length uses shapely.ops.substring to cut any line longer than a threshold into bounded pieces.



Spatial index (.sindex)
An R-tree index over a layer’s bounding boxes, so that “which geometries are near this one?” is resolved in approximately \(O(\log n)\) instead of comparing against every other geometry one by one. This is what keeps split_streets_at_intersections and the nearest-street lookups tractable at CDMX scale (hundreds of thousands of segments).


Bounding box filtering
A cheap prefilter before a more expensive operation: keep only the rows whose coordinates fall within a rectangle —either directly, df["lat"].between(lat_lo, lat_hi) & df["lon"].between(lon_lo, lon_hi) (geo_split from src/eda/core.py), or with geopandas’ own .cx[xmin:xmax, ymin:ymax] indexer.


Aggregation by geometry
Spatial join, then groupby, then merge the polygons back —the pattern behind every “crime count by district/street/year” table in this repository (cvegeo_aggregate, street_aggregate in src/eda/core.py).

title: Appendix — Geospatial Data Structures and Operations
text:
Raster to Vector Aggregation (Pixel Coverage)
This is the central geospatial technique of the whole project: converting a raster (the AlphaEarth pixel grid) into a single vector for a vector geometry (a street, a polygon).



Pixel coverage logic for Political Division


The recipe is the same regardless of whether the target geometry is a polygon or a line (src/etl/assign_point_to_geometry.py, src/etl/get_training_sets.py):

Find every pixel (its center, treated as a point) that touches the target geometry.
Average the 64-dimensional embedding vectors of that coverage.
L2-normalize the averaged vector, so that the aggregate lands back on the unit sphere (\(S^{63}\)) on which AlphaEarth embeddings are natively defined —the average of unit vectors is not itself a unit vector.

normalize(df[feat_cols], norm="l2", axis=1)

Streaming large rasters
The raw AlphaEarth GeoTIFFs are too large to be loaded whole into memory. tif_to_parquet_partition from src/etl/process_embeddings.py reads them in fixed-size sliding windows (rasterio.windows.Window), masks the nodata pixels, recovers the true (lon, lat) of each pixel with rasterio.transform.xy, and appends each window as a chunk to a partitioned parquet dataset —converting an arbitrarily large raster to tabular form in bounded memory.
crumbs: Appendix — Geospatial Data Structures and Operations

title: Appendix — Geospatial Data Structures and Operations
text:
Large-Scale Geospatial-Tabular Storage: Hive Partitioning
The processed embeddings (tens of millions of rows, at whole-city level) are stored as a Hive-style partitioned parquet dataset —one subfolder per year=/CVE_MUN= combination— so that the code can read, or sample, only the partitions it actually needs:
dataset = pyarrow.dataset.dataset(path, format="parquet", partitioning="hive")
dataset.count_rows()                # metadata only, no data read
fragment.to_table(columns=[...])    # one partition at a time
src/visuals/embedding_structure_showcase.py uses exactly this to draw a random, representative sample of the whole city without ever keeping the full ~15.9M-row dataset in memory at once.
crumbs: Appendix — Geospatial Data Structures and Operations

title: Appendix — Geospatial Data Structures and Operations
text:
Spatial Clustering and Density

DBSCAN
Def: DBSCAN is a density-based clustering algorithm —a point with at least min_samples neighbors within a radius eps anchors a cluster; everything else is labeled as noise. Because eps is a real distance, DBSCAN has to run over a projected CRS (EPSG:6372 here), never over raw lat/lon degrees (gif_dbscan_by_year from src/eda/core.py).


Concave / convex hull
Used to outline the shape of a cluster once DBSCAN has assigned the labels: shapely.concave_hull, falling back to the plain .convex_hull for very small clusters or where concave_hull is not available.


Kernel Density Estimation (KDE)
A smoothed density surface over the point coordinates (seaborn.kdeplot), used as a lighter alternative to clustering when the goal is just to see where incidents concentrate, not to assign each point a discrete label.


Spherical K-means
Not a spatial operation in the strict coordinate sense —it groups embedding vectors, not (lat, lon) points— but it shares the unit-sphere logic of the pixel aggregation step: the features are L2-normalized first, so that the Euclidean distance between cluster centroids becomes a monotone function of the cosine similarity. See src/unsupervised/clustering_kmeans.py.
crumbs: Appendix — Geospatial Data Structures and Operations

title: Appendix — Geospatial Data Structures and Operations
text:
Basemaps
For a static map that needs real-world visual context (streets, neighborhoods, labels) instead of just bare outlines, contextily.add_basemap fetches CartoDB/OpenStreetMap tiles and draws them behind the vector layers —but only once everything is in Web Mercator (src/visuals/flash_highlight_showcase.py):
gdf_3857 = gdf.to_crs(3857)
gdf_3857.plot(ax=ax)
contextily.add_basemap(ax, source=contextily.providers.CartoDB.Positron, crs=gdf_3857.crs)
crumbs: Appendix — Geospatial Data Structures and Operations

title: Appendix — Geospatial Data Structures and Operations
text:
Choropleth Maps
Def: a choropleth map fills each polygon or line with a color based on an attribute value, gdf.plot(column="y_cnt", cmap=..., vmin=..., vmax=...), instead of plotting raw points. It is used throughout this repository for incident count maps, risk level maps and cluster maps —always paired with a fixed color scale (vmin/vmax, or a BoundaryNorm for discrete levels), so that the panels stay comparable across frames and years.

title: Appendix — Fundamental Models, Metrics and Algorithms
text: This appendix gathers brief descriptions of the models, evaluation metrics and fundamental mathematical/computational building blocks used throughout this repository, each with a link to a basic, validated reference (mostly Wikipedia) for anyone who wants to go one level deeper. Like the other appendices, this is not a general ML textbook, just what is actually used in the code.
crumbs: Appendix — Fundamental Models, Metrics and Algorithms

title: Appendix — Fundamental Models, Metrics and Algorithms
text:
Models
Logistic Regression — a linear model for a binary outcome: it fits a linear combination of the features and squashes it through the sigmoid function to produce a probability, \(P(y=1\mid x) = \sigma(x^{\top}\beta)\) with \(\sigma(z) = \tfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\). It is used as the simplest baseline classifier for the “did this street report any incident?” target (src/supervised/models/clf_logreg.py). See Logistic regression.
Gradient Boosted Trees (XGBoost) — an ensemble of shallow decision trees built sequentially, where each new tree fits the residual errors (gradient) of the ensemble so far. It is used both for classification (clf_xgb.py) and, with a Poisson/Negative-Binomial/hurdle objective, for count regression (reg_xgb.py). See Gradient boosting and XGBoost.
Neural Network Heads (MLP) — a Multilayer Perceptron, a stack of fully connected layers with a non-linear activation between them, trained end-to-end over the embedding vector. It is used as the third model family for both the classification and the count targets (clf_nn.py, reg_nn.py), trained via backpropagation (see below). See Multilayer perceptron.
Poisson / Negative Binomial / Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression — regression models for a non-negative integer (count) outcome, instead of the continuous outcome assumed by ordinary least squares. Plain Poisson assumes \(P(Y=k) = \tfrac{\mu^{k} e^{-\mu}}{k!}\) with \(\mu = e^{x^{\top}\beta}\); Negative Binomial adds an overdispersion parameter on top of plain Poisson, and Zero-Inflated Poisson (ZIP) additionally mixes in an extra probability mass \(\pi\) at zero, \(P(Y=0) = \pi + (1-\pi)e^{-\mu}\) and \(P(Y=k>0) = (1-\pi)\tfrac{\mu^{k}e^{-\mu}}{k!}\). It is used for the count target \(y_{cnt}\), since crime counts per street are exactly this: non-negative, integer and dominated by zeros. See Poisson regression and Zero-inflated model.
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) — a linear dimensionality reduction technique that finds the orthogonal directions (components) of maximum variance in the data. It is used throughout src/unsupervised/dim_reduction.py and in the embedding structure showcase as the default way to visualize the embedding space in 2-3 dimensions. See Principal component analysis.
t-SNE — a non-linear dimensionality reduction technique that preserves local neighborhood structure, good for revealing clusters that PCA’s linear projection may hide. It is used in src/unsupervised/manifold_learning.py, always over a bounded sample, since it does not scale to millions of rows. See T-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding.
UMAP — another non-linear dimensionality reduction technique, built on a different mathematical foundation (manifold learning / topological data analysis) than t-SNE, generally faster and better at preserving some of the global structure alongside the local one. It is used in compute_umap of manifold_learning.py, fitted on a sample and then applied to the rest of the data in batches. See UMAP.
Locally Linear Embedding (LLE) — a manifold learning technique that reconstructs each point as a weighted combination of its nearest neighbors, and then finds a lower-dimensional embedding that best preserves those local weights. It is used in compute_lle of manifold_learning.py. See Nonlinear dimensionality reduction.
Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) — places points in a low-dimensional space so that their pairwise distances match, as faithfully as possible, the original pairwise distances in the full feature space. It is used in compute_mds of manifold_learning.py, bounded to a small sample, since it needs the full pairwise distance matrix. See Multidimensional scaling.
K-means (spherical variant) — an iterative clustering algorithm that assigns each point to its nearest centroid out of \(k\), and then recomputes each centroid as the mean of its assigned points, until convergence. It is used in src/unsupervised/clustering_kmeans.py via MiniBatchKMeans (see mini-batch algorithms below), with the centroids renormalized to the unit sphere after each update, so that Euclidean distance behaves like cosine distance —the “spherical” adaptation appropriate for the normalized AlphaEarth embeddings. See K-means clustering.
DBSCAN — a density-based clustering algorithm: a point with enough neighbors within a given radius anchors a cluster, and everything else that cannot be reached this way is labeled as noise, with no need to fix the number of clusters beforehand. It is used in gif_dbscan_by_year of src/eda/core.py over the projected (metric) crime coordinates. See DBSCAN.

title: Appendix — Fundamental Models, Metrics and Algorithms
text:
Metrics
Notation, in what follows: \(TP, FP, FN, TN\) are the confusion matrix cells (true/false positives/negatives); \(y_i \in \{0,1\}\) is the true label (or \(y_i \in \mathbb{N}\) for counts), \(\hat{y}_i\) the predicted value and \(p_i \in [0,1]\) the predicted probability, over \(N\) observations.
ROC curve / ROC-AUC — the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate across all thresholds; the area under it (AUC) summarizes the ranking quality in a single number, largely insensitive to class imbalance. Equivalently, \(\mathrm{AUC} = P\big(s(x^{+}) > s(x^{-})\big)\) for a random positive/negative pair with scores \(s\). See Receiver operating characteristic.
Precision, Recall and F1 score — precision is the proportion of predicted positives that are correct, recall is the proportion of actual positives that were found, and F1 is their harmonic mean:
\[ \mathrm{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}, \qquad \mathrm{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}, \qquad F_1 = \frac{2\,\mathrm{Precision}\cdot\mathrm{Recall}}{\mathrm{Precision}+\mathrm{Recall}}. \]
Reported at a fixed threshold of 0.5 and across a full threshold scenario table for the classification models. See Precision and recall.
PR-AUC / Average Precision — the area under the Precision-Recall curve; unlike ROC-AUC, it does not average over the (very large) count of true negatives, which makes it the most informative summary here, given how imbalanced the crime indicator is. In its Average Precision form, \(\mathrm{AP} = \sum_k (R_k - R_{k-1})\,P_k\), a weighted sum of precisions \(P_k\) over the recall increments \(R_k - R_{k-1}\). It is also the metric against which Optuna tunes the classifiers. See Average precision.
Balanced Accuracy — the average of the recall obtained on each class, correcting the bias of plain accuracy toward the majority class under imbalance: \(\tfrac{1}{2}\big(\mathrm{TPR} + \mathrm{TNR}\big)\), with \(\mathrm{TPR} = \tfrac{TP}{TP+FN}\) and \(\mathrm{TNR} = \tfrac{TN}{TN+FP}\). See Accuracy and precision.
Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) — a single correlation-like score between \(-1\) and \(1\) computed from all four confusion matrix cells at once, considered a robust summary even under strong class imbalance:
\[ \mathrm{MCC} = \frac{TP\cdot TN - FP\cdot FN}{\sqrt{(TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)}}. \]
See Phi coefficient.
Log loss (cross-entropy) — penalizes a probability forecast by the negative log-likelihood it assigns to the true outcome, rewarding not only a correct class but well-calibrated confidence: \(-\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big[y_i\log p_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\big]\). See Cross-entropy.
Brier score — the mean squared error between a predicted probability and the actual outcome (0/1), \(\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(p_i - y_i)^2\); another calibration-sensitive companion to the ranking metrics above. See Brier score.
Poisson deviance — a goodness-of-fit measure for count models, comparing the fitted mean \(\hat{\mu}_i\) against the observed count \(y_i\) under the Poisson likelihood, \(D = 2\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big[y_i\log\tfrac{y_i}{\hat{\mu}_i} - (y_i - \hat{\mu}_i)\big]\); used here as the main tuning metric for the count regression models. See Deviance (statistics).
MAE / RMSE — Mean Absolute Error and Root Mean Square Error, the two standard scale-dependent error summaries for the predicted versus observed count, \(\mathrm{MAE} = \tfrac{1}{N}\sum_i |y_i - \hat{y}_i|\) and \(\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}\), reported alongside the Poisson deviance. See Mean absolute error and Root mean square deviation.
Spearman rank correlation — correlation between the ranks of two variables instead of their raw values, \(\rho = 1 - \tfrac{6\sum_i d_i^2}{n(n^2-1)}\) with \(d_i\) the difference in ranks (for distinct ranks); it is used to check whether the predicted count at least orders the streets correctly, even where the absolute count is hard to pin down. See Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient.
Silhouette score — for each point \(i\), it compares its average distance \(a_i\) to the points of its own cluster against its distance \(b_i\) to the nearest different cluster, \(s_i = \tfrac{b_i - a_i}{\max(a_i, b_i)}\); averaged over all points, it is one of the diagnostics used to choose \(k\) in the k-means sweep. See Silhouette (clustering).
Calinski-Harabasz index — the ratio between the between-cluster dispersion and the within-cluster dispersion, \(\mathrm{CH} = \tfrac{\operatorname{tr}(B_k)/(k-1)}{\operatorname{tr}(W_k)/(N-k)}\) with \(B_k\), \(W_k\) the between- and within-cluster dispersion matrices; higher is better separated, and it is cheap enough to compute over the full dataset (unlike silhouette, which is subsampled here). See Calinski–Harabasz index.
Davies-Bouldin index — the average similarity between each cluster and its most similar cluster, \(\mathrm{DB} = \tfrac{1}{k}\sum_{i}\max_{j\neq i}\tfrac{s_i + s_j}{d_{ij}}\) with \(s_i\) the within-cluster dispersion and \(d_{ij}\) the distance between centroids; lower is better separated. It is used alongside silhouette and Calinski-Harabasz in the \(k\) selection sweep. See Davies–Bouldin index.
Kruskal-Wallis H test — a non-parametric test of whether several groups (here, the k-means clusters) come from the same outcome distribution, without assuming normality. Because the sample sizes here are enormous (hundreds of thousands of streets), the \(p\) value collapses to zero for almost any real effect, so the pipeline reports the effect size \(\epsilon^2 = \tfrac{H - k + 1}{N - k}\) derived from the test statistic \(H\) instead of just \(p\). See Kruskal–Wallis test.

title: Appendix — Fundamental Models, Metrics and Algorithms
text:
Basic Mathematics and Computing Algorithms
Cosine similarity and L2 normalization — the angle-based similarity between two vectors, and the operation that rescales a vector to unit length. Both are covered extensively, with their formal definitions, in Chapter 2; they reappear here as the reason why k-means runs in its spherical form and the reason why the pixel coverage aggregation (see Geospatial Data Appendix) renormalizes after averaging.
Gradient Descent and Backpropagation — gradient descent is the general recipe for minimizing a loss function by taking repeated steps in the direction opposite to its gradient; backpropagation is the efficient algorithm that computes that gradient for each weight in a neural network through the chain rule, layer by layer. This is how the NN heads (clf_nn.py, reg_nn.py) are trained, via torch.optim.Adam, an adaptive variant of gradient descent. See Gradient descent and Backpropagation.
Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and its randomized variant — SVD factorizes any matrix into rotation/scaling/rotation components; PCA is, deep down, an SVD of the (centered) data matrix. Because an exact SVD is too slow for millions of rows, sklearn’s PCA(svd_solver="randomized") is used instead, an approximate algorithm that reaches a comparable decomposition much faster using random projections. See Singular value decomposition and Randomized algorithm.
K-fold Cross-Validation (group-aware) — the standard recipe of splitting the data into \(k\) folds, training on \(k-1\) and validating on the held-out one, repeating \(k\) times. This pipeline uses a group variant (src/supervised/cv.py), where each (year, municipality) cell stays entirely within a single fold, so that no street’s information leaks across the train/validation split by way of its neighbors. See Cross-validation (statistics).
Bayesian hyperparameter search (TPE) — instead of a grid or random search, src/supervised/tuning.py uses Optuna’s Tree-structured Parzen Estimator, a Bayesian optimization method that builds a probabilistic model of “which hyperparameters tend to give good results” from the trials seen so far, and uses it to propose more promising candidates for the next trial. See Bayesian optimization.
Mini-batch stochastic optimization — instead of recomputing an update from the whole dataset, the model is repeatedly updated from small random batches, which is both cheaper per step and, for very large datasets, the only tractable option. MiniBatchKMeans (the engine behind the spherical k-means above) applies exactly this idea to the classic k-means update. See Stochastic gradient descent.

title: Conclusions
text: Here we share some of the derived learnings that emerged from the data, the models and, most importantly, from the work and the completion of this exercise.

title: Conclusions
text:
Learnings about Embeddings
Aggregations and the raster representation of continuous, not well-defined geometric objects (such as buildings, streets, etc.) turned out to be key to actually recovering valuable open and direct data at scale from our objects of interest. Without sensible aggregation and assignment logic, embeddings simply do not translate into something a street or a polygon can use as a feature.
We also learned that understanding the original training architecture and the training data used behind the embeddings helps to understand both their advantages and their limitations; it is not enough to simply consume the vectors as a black box: knowing what the model was exposed to during training tells us what it can and cannot represent well.
Finally, embeddings include a large amount of implicit features of places, so we have to be careful when understanding the similarities between really different places in the same city. Two streets can look close in embedding space for reasons that have nothing to do with crime, so scaling up on similarity comparisons and other variable enrichments (socio-demographic, land use, etc.) is key to interpreting them correctly.

title: Conclusions
section: Learnings from Crime Data and Models
text:
Learnings from Crime Data and Models
Real data is messy, and crime data is even messier. Bias, low data quality and records that are not consistently updated can affect the results of the models and their applications, no matter how correct the implementation, training and interpretation are. Working with the official crime reports made this very concrete: under-reporting and inconsistent updates are not isolated cases, they are the norm around which we have to design.
That is why it is important to use the data as evidence and as an auxiliary tool, always considering the nature of the problem at hand. In this case, that means understanding that criminal behavior is not based solely on observable data; there are structural, social and political factors that no dataset captures completely, so the models are meant to inform, not to replace, that broader judgment.

title: Conclusions
text:
What was found?
Crime does not occur in a completely random way. Despite being a complex phenomenon, features such as embeddings allow us to show that we can understand meaningful patterns in crime based on the features of the terrain and of space; the risk levels built from the models are not noise, they align with recognizable geography.
There are also some interesting patterns in terms of risk levels; for example, some of the riskiest zones include both highly developed urban areas and low-development areas alike, and this seems to be explained by different mechanisms for each one: low-development areas tend to resort to crime as a way of accessing resources, while highly developed areas seem to be target places for crimes to occur.
Finally, embeddings used as a covariate together with other socio-demographic features can improve model performance; they are not meant to replace census or socioeconomic data, but to complement it with the spatial and structural signal that those variables by themselves do not carry.

title: Conclusions
text:
Future work and improvements
Many things to improve in the current flow have already been detected; without being exhaustive, the following list:
The most obvious: it is clear that opportunistic bias is present; the riskiest areas have a strong correlation with populated areas. However, the solution is not straightforward; it is not enough to simply compute per capita rates, since the embeddings also contain information about geography that correlates with human activity and, therefore, with population, so normalization is not trivial and deserves dedicated treatment of its own.
The assignment logic can also become smarter, not only through direct assignment via the nearest object, but also by including a weighted logic that takes into account how much of an object actually overlaps or is located near each street or polygon, instead of a hard nearest-neighbor cutoff.
Formal statistical tests on the clustering algorithms are required to scale the conclusions and to really treat clustering modeling as useful.
Finally, dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA work well with normally distributed data, and here it is used mainly as a visualization tool to show the features of the embedding representation in a low-dimensional view, rather than as a rigorous statistical projection, so there is room to explore techniques better suited to the actual distribution of the embeddings.

title: Embeddings Applications on Crime
text:
The power of embeddings to enrich models and to give the opportunity to create geospatial analytics with just one target variable was mentioned in Chapter 2.
Most applications come from Earth sciences, economic dynamics and logistics; there is a great opportunity to understand social and political behavior in general, but particularly for the use of embeddings in the social and political sciences. In the case of this work we will try to apply it to understanding crime in Mexico City.

title: Embeddings Applications on Crime
text:
Modeling Crime
One of the most challenging problems in the social sciences is modeling crime, and this is due to the complexity and the multidisciplinary nature of crime.
Starting with data caveats such as under-reporting, false reports, bureaucratic friction and data mismatch, not to mention corruption and public perception biases.
Then problems also arise when using earth embeddings and other environmental variables in social science research, for example the opportunistic bias, that is, where there is more population there is also more incidence and propensity to commit crimes.
Another important thing to know is that the approach here, despite the training and evaluation target or feature, in the end does not seek to predict per se the crime incidents that will occur on the streets, but to use the predictive outputs to evaluate risk levels and suggest strategies to our stakeholders (whether these are government agencies, decision makers or researchers).
So, even though the models are ultimately used to predict incidents on new data, the final goal is to label the objects of interest under a risk tier and to use the model not as a crystal ball, but as an auxiliary tool to understand crime patterns based on structural, geographic and environmental features.

Decisions to model
When working on models there are a series of decisions that are part of the modeling and of the system design for a model; it is not only about selecting the model, but also about aligning the data definitions and gathering the elements required to perform an analysis. For example, for this particular modeling there are the following challenges:

Different geospatial aggregations and point geometries of the elements (Rasters/polygons) for the embeddings, versus the point (coordinate) geometry for the crime incident reports.
Variations in the data boundaries: Validating the correct coordinate entries of both the embedding data and the point data within the official political division for the territorial delimitation of the city.
Defining the model(s) and target variables to exploit the embedding data for predictive and inference tasks.

Thus, the modeling decisions to be made would be the following:

Definition of the target variable (crime events, crime events per population, etc.)
Definitions of the appropriate geographic aggregation level.
Data pipelines and quality checks.
Data-generating models (model type families and hyperparameters for each one, evaluation metrics).

Each model approach will take these factors into account and will be presented in each scenario.


Data processing and aggregation
To run the data flow and the training, it is assumed that the following files are already downloaded and saved in the appropriate directories based on the code paths:

CDMX street geometry [SHP]: Download from INEGI’s Marco Geoestadístico. Or any other polygon of interest (See building units or MZA).
FGJ Carpetas [CSV]: CSV database with geocoded crime incidences (lat/lon points), from the area of interest.
Google Earth Embeddings.

The reason why the databases are not provided, nor is there executable production code (although we include the scripts needed to run and obtain the data), goes beyond a volume issue: for the crime datasets, changes in the public datasets make the endpoints unstable, while INEGI and Google Earth are highly reliable sources in terms of data and APIs; for this particular set of geometries and raster assets an instance of manual interaction with the user interface is needed. But the codes provided in these notes and in the repository remain highly reliable.

Usual (implicit) assumptions
There are some particular assumptions that come from using earth embeddings as a proxy or covariates in a crime analysis, some of the most important in terms of structural definition.

Assumption 1: Crime is structural
One assumption is that the natural, geographic, economic, political and security features of neighborhoods and regions predispose the population to commit crimes or to be victims of them.
Despite the well-founded criticism that crime itself impacts the population, the dynamics and the development of the region, we will work with a valid assumption of the constant feedback loop:



Crime-conditions Feedback Loop


An analysis of how much each component impacts the other and of how the temporal dynamics work is outside the scope of the present analysis. However, it is a compulsory and necessary additional research that must be carried out to understand the problem.
Therefore, the expected causal relationships we are exploring here are defined as follows (assumption):

It is important to review how embeddings are conceptualized as a representation of the features of space:

Source: Google DeepMind — AlphaEarth Foundations.
As we can see, the assumption is that the embeddings for a given region capture multiple environmental changes and dynamics of the given terrain during the year, satellite sensors and multiple image processings of the region, therefore they also capture multiple structural features such as infrastructure, human activity, regional climate, etc.
Sometimes the data is not available or is not reliable for one or more of these factors for a certain region, for example:

\[ y_{\text{crime}} = f(\text{embedding})\]
Where \(y_{\text{crime}}\) could be either an indicator of crime incidents or even the amount of expected crime incidents that would be reported in a spatial unit over a time span.

title: Embeddings Applications on Crime
text:
Data Processing

Object-level aggregation
For the following model, we will use the mugging data aggregated by street, understanding by street the street segment between corners, with the following logic:

We assign each crime incident to the street closest to the point of occurrence.
For the socio-demographic data, we assign to each street the value of the MZA centroid that is closest to that street.
Finally, to assign the embedding values, we take the coverage raster mosaic that completely covers the street and then average them and normalize to 1 (to keep the embedding norm based on AlphaEarth), assigning that value to the street.

In addition, the training process consists of the following models, each of which was trained with the following logic:

Grouped K-fold validation at the year and municipality level.
Leaving out 2 municipalities and one year for an out-of-sample evaluation of the trained models.
The feature columns that are not part of the embedding layers were minimally processed, only in order to observe the lift generated over a plain dataset by adding the embedding layers.

It is important to note that, in the case where we have a continuous geospatial variable of interest (in this case coordinates with crimes), it is important to select the correct aggregation level that has a real interpretation in the field, not just a convenient data aggregation; take for example the following figure:



Data Level Aggregations


In black dots, the coordinates of the reported crimes, and different aggregations using Google Earth buildings and the official street geometries. We would like to match the street crime, such as Asalto a transeúnte (mugging), or even the building/MZA aggregation for Robo a casa habitación (home burglary).
Hence the street-level assignment rule as a pivot is followed:

Crime: The point (incidence) is assigned to the line (street) closest in Euclidean distance (after applying a projection onto a metric space).
Block (Manzana) data: The values reported by INEGI at the MZA level are assigned by attributing to the street the values of the block whose centroid is closest to the street in a Euclidean sense (after the corresponding metric projection).
Embedding: An aggregation (average) of all the embeddings covering the street is performed (see the following Figure 21) and they are normalized.

The following figure exemplifies the assignment logic for building the street training set.



Geospatial assignment rules to streets with other data in different geometries.




Training dataset
The final feature dataset to be included is composed of 3 databases:

The full 64 AlphaEarth Embeddings.
A selection of Socio-demographic Data.
Target variable for the count: \(y_{count}\).
Target variable for the classification: \(y_{ind}\).

All aggregated at the street level.

Model Fitting: Supervised Learning Methods
Following the plug and play patterns described in Chapter 2, the supervised approach takes the street-level training set, embeddings plus a selection of socio-demographic covariates, and fits a model \(\hat{f}\) against one of the two target variables defined above: the count \(y_{count}\) (how many incidents were reported on that street in that year) or the indicator \(y_{ind}\) (whether at least one occurred).
For each target we benchmark three model families, from the simplest linear plug-in to a learned non-linear head, across the same three feature sets (embeddings only, other covariates only, and both combined), so that the lift attributable to the embeddings themselves is directly comparable:

Count regression: since the crime counts per street are zero-inflated (most streets report none, a few report many), we fit XGBoost and a Neural Network count head, both under a Zero-Inflated Poisson specification (and related families), instead of a plain linear or Poisson regression.
Classification: the same feature sets, but fitted against the binary indicator \(y_{ind}\) with Logistic Regression, XGBoost and a Neural Network head, given the highly imbalanced nature of the target.

Each model is trained with group-aware K-fold validation (grouped by year and municipality, so that no street leaks between folds) and is evaluated on a reserved year and pair of municipalities never seen during training, following the data processing logic described above.

It is important to emphasize that these models were trained with three data tables: socioeconomic data (INEGI), 64−dim AlphaEarth Embeddings and both simultaneously, optimizing hyperparameters over each group of variables on their own. Count regression
Regression for counts constitutes a generalization of the linear model (within the Generalized Linear Models, GLM, framework) oriented to fitting discrete occurrence events. Given the nature of crime events —intrinsically a count of occurrences in space and time— it is natural to model that occurrence \(y\) through a Poisson distribution or related distributions for count variables (for example, Negative Binomial), where the target variable \(y\) takes values in the non-negative integers, that is,
\[
y \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}.
\]
In particular, crime events are considered rare in terms of occurrence frequency, and the evidence from the exploratory analysis confirms an over-representation of null values (excess zeros) relative to what is expected under a standard Poisson or Negative Binomial. For this reason, a zero-inflated discrete model is chosen, whose probability mass function is defined piecewise as
\[
P(Y = y) =
\begin{cases}
\pi + (1-\pi)\, f_Y(0 \mid \theta), & y = 0, \\[4pt]
(1-\pi)\, f_Y(y \mid \theta), & y \in \{1, 2, 3, \dots\},
\end{cases}
\]
where:

\(\pi \in [0,1]\) is the probability that the observation comes from the structural zero component, that is, from the over-representation of null observations extraneous to the count process itself.
\(1-\pi\) is the probability that the observation comes from the count-generating process itself, that is, from the subset of cases in which the criminal phenomenon actually occurs, and \(f_Y(\cdot \mid \theta)\) determines how many events are observed.
\(f_Y(\cdot \mid \theta)\) is the probability mass function of the data-generating process, parameterized by \(\theta\).

In this work, the Poisson and Negative Binomial distributions are used as base distributions for \(f_Y(\cdot \mid \theta)\), and they are additionally contrasted with Hurdle-type models as an alternative specification for handling the excess of zeros.
It is important to mention that the boosting method is used for computational efficiency. For a better and more appropriate fit it is advisable to use Bayesian modeling and libraries such as STAN for the modeling flow. That said, it is important to highlight that this approach does not directly fit the zero-inflated models but, in order to achieve an equivalent fit, it is done in two parts: a first classification fit and then a regression over the positive cases.
Moreover, a Bayesian application is hardly interpretable given the nature of the features in the embeddings, so we would not be gaining interpretability and we would be losing compute time. If one wanted to study random effects per street, then a Bayesian model should indeed be fitted, but the number of parameters to estimate makes it intractable; a CAR model could be used for spatial autocorrelation, but that is not necessary because of the implicit spatial correlation assumptions in the embeddings.



Regression Result for Zero-Inflated Poisson XGB,





Counts for Zero-Inflated Poisson NN Head





Count for holdout for Counting Regression


As we can see, the predicted performance seems to be really close to the real values when predicting the zero-inflated incidence for crime at the street level. Here, a particular risk could be the overfitting of our model. And also an under-representation of rare event counts, that is, for streets with incidence greater than \(3\). A tuning via regularization is needed to address this problem.
Despite having an overfit at the values 0 and near-zero such as 1 and 2, when saying that the model has correctly fitted the discrete target variable \(Y ∈\{0,1,2,3,...\}\), one could say that the model has learned to classify between very likely incidence (positive incidence) and no incidence, ignoring extreme cases. While work can be done to improve the results insofar as it is a regression model, the nature of the problem demands thinking about the training beyond a point prediction, toward an application of the regression as an instrument for assessing incidence risk. As future work it is suggested to investigate the use of conformal prediction to create confidence intervals from these models.


Classification on event occurrence
In this part, we train the model only with an indicator variable: whether or not a street had any recorded crime throughout the year.
We then train the same model families, but for a binary classification problem with imbalanced classes (given the zero-inflated behavior present in crime incidence).
It is important to recall what the objective of binary classification is insofar as it is a supervised learning algorithm: in this case, the response variable \(Y\) does not correspond to the number of incidents, but to the fact that, given an element —in this case, a street— it is identified with \(Y=1\) if there was at least one recorded crime, or with \(Y=0\) if no incident was recorded. Formally,
\[
Y =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if the street recorded at least one crime in the period,} \\
0, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
In this work a binary classification problem is thus posed: given a set of features \(\mathbb{X}\), we seek to find a function \(g\) such that
\[
g: \mathbb{X} \longrightarrow \{0,1\},
\]
and the classifier is defined as
\[
f(x \mid \theta) =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if } g(x) \geq \tau, \\
0, & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}
\]
where \(\tau\) is the decision threshold. The parameters \(\theta\) are fitted so as to minimize the objective function
\[
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{L}\left(y_i, f(x_i \mid \theta)\right) + \lambda\, R(\theta),
\]
where \(\mathbb{L}\) is a loss function, \(R\) a regularization function, and \(\lambda \geq 0\) the parameter that controls the relative weight of that regularization.
Subsequently, we train the same model families, now under the approach of a binary classification problem with imbalanced classes, given the zero-inflated behavior characteristic of crime incidence.
In the following figures, one can observe the performance results on a sample not seen in training and reserved exclusively for validation for the different classification configurations, that is, the different models, described in Table \(1\), with different data groups: \(1)\) socioeconomic data (other), \(2)\) embeddings, \(3)\) both (combined).

Now, after reviewing the data obtained from the evaluation and plotted in the previous Figures, we can conclude two important points, one bad and one good piece of news, that is, the following:
Did the model learn to classify? No. Given the level of imbalance of the samples, the model can reach a high level of recall simply by selecting the majority class, although at a very high cost in precision. If we consider the set of Precision-Recall curves, the story they tell is consistent: the cost in precision for recovering correct positive cases is too high, so that to recover barely \(20\%\) of the positive cases, all models sit at around \(10\%\) precision.
Returning to the classification point, given a trained model \(\hat{f}\), the loss function or empirical error
\[
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left| \hat{f}(x_i) - y_i \right|
\]
does not reach a value low enough for the model to be usable in practical applications with a direct interpretation of the classification.
Were the embeddings of any use? However, what we can see is that, at least when embeddings are used, the model’s performance improves. Consider that the incidence or not of a crime between one street and another, particularly for low-incidence elements, could be circumstantial rather than systemic. Moreover, being strict with the interpretation of the ROC-AUC curve, and abusing this interpretation, the model improves the decision of cataloguing a street as risky or not compared to a random selection, but noting that it is not enough to propose an as is solution. This must be consulted with a subject-matter expert; in technical terms and proper to the training, the classification is poor, but the value it brings and the tolerance for false positives, among others, remains subject to the determination of the subject-matter expert for a final decision or implementation.


Benchmarks
From the following figures, we can conclude that both NN and XGBoost perform better than logistic regression for Classification, and for Count Regression, both XGB and NN are quite similar under the same dataset, both with Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression, while there is clearly a large gain in the evaluation metrics with the datasets that include vector embeddings.



Feature set metric comparison in Holdout





Feature set metric comparison in Out of Sample CV





ROC-AUC Model Comparison

title: Embeddings Applications on Crime
section: Discovering Hidden Patterns: Unsupervised Learning Methods
text:
Discovering Hidden Patterns: Unsupervised Learning Methods
Unlike the supervised approach, here there is no target variable to fit against; we only have the embedding (and covariate) feature space itself, and the question changes from “can we predict \(y\)?” to “does the feature space, by itself, organize the streets into meaningfully distinct groups?”. This matters for crime modeling precisely because of the archetype logic introduced above: if streets with similar structural and environmental features (as captured by the embeddings) group together regardless of their reported incidence, then that structure can be used to flag riskier streets even where incidents are under-reported or simply have not occurred yet, using neighborhood in the feature space as a proxy for risk instead of the historical count alone.
We approach this in two complementary ways, both purely on the feature space: first, dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE and other manifold learning methods) to visualize whether high- and low-incidence streets already separate in a low-dimensional projection; and second, clustering (spherical K-means) to assign each street, reported or not, to a discrete group that can afterwards be characterized and ordered by risk.

Dimensionality Reduction
First, since we have a series of unlabeled features, a first step is to perform a series of dimensionality reductions to visualize the potential of the embeddings to group or characterize the data, particularly keeping the meaning in the context of the crimes committed on the streets.

Principal Component Analysis



PCA for each street colored by yearly incidences


As we can see, by reducing the dimensionality we can see that the records or streets with high incidence show a grouping that could be characterized through clustering models or other unsupervised algorithms.


t-SNE



t-SNE for Alpha Earth embeddings from 2022 to 2024


Here we also see some kind of grouping by incidence level, and since t-SNE is an algorithm that keeps both local and global similarity, we will check whether clustering can generate a characterization for crime hotspots.


SVD



SVD projection of Alpha Earth embeddings by year, colored by incidence


Here we can observe another powerful technique for matrix factorization called Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), which is a generalization of the eigenvector decomposition, sometimes used as a data compression (dimensionality reduction) technique consisting of geometric operations: rotation, scaling and rotation. We can observe the nature of the embeddings and the dispersion patterns for the crime occurrence values. Since, deep down, most large-scale PCA operations use a form of SVD, we continue using PCA as our main dimensionality reduction technique. However, deeper future research on this decomposition could be valuable.



Manifold Learning
Also known as Non-linear Dimensionality Reduction techniques, these are further dimensionality reduction techniques where, in contrast, for example, with PCA, the reduction does not occur through a linear process but via kernel factorization and optimization techniques. Some of them are presented here to see whether any interesting pattern is revealed in a non-linear space with respect to the embedding values related to street-level crime incidence.



UMAP for Alpha Earth embeddings from 2022 to 2024





LLE for Alpha Earth embeddings from 2022 to 2024


For the first UMAP model, a pattern can be observed in the upper section of the learned surface. In the LLE projection shown, it appears that most of the streets with high incidences are associated with features in the learned space that are located in the same collinear section.
This tells us that, although we are not making any inference, it appears that in the dimensionality reduction we find that streets with high incidences seem to be close in space, both in the original embedding features and in learned spaces. From here arises the possibility of experimenting with the following modeling strategies or architectures:

Direct: K-means or direct grouping between vectors (risk of variance due to the curse of dimensionality). Particularly, K-means, as explained in this work, works well with high dimension by reducing the distance from the original dimension to a scalar difference by means of the cosine distance on the sphere (where the embeddings live).
Dimensionality reduction + Grouping: dimension reduction allows keeping as much information as possible and having values in low, manageable dimensions; depending on the Dimensionality Reduction model, the computational cost could be restrictive. It is suggested to use k nearest neighbors or models such as DBSCAN as grouping, given the low cost at scale and the interpretability.

It is important to highlight that the statistical validity of the clustering lies in performing hypothesis tests to determine the distributional difference of the clusters; methods such as the Energy Distance and such tests will be omitted as they fall outside the scope of the present work and because of their computational cost at this data scale.


Clustering
To perform clustering at such a large scale of points, and considering that the given data comes from a normalized interval \([-1,1]\), the most direct path to obtain a clustering from the embeddings is via k-Means clustering on the sphere (equivalent to cosine spherical K-means clustering, given that it is normalized).

To interpret the results in order to clarify them for a stakeholder, for example, we would divide the clusters into the following 3 risk levels:

High-risk streets: Those within the cluster with the highest maximum number of occurrences.
Moderate: The two intermediate ones in order of maximum number of occurrences.
Low-risk streets: Those within the cluster with the lowest maximum number of occurrences.

An appropriate final conclusion to confirm that the clustering is really identifying statistically different groups is to apply multivariate distribution tests to statistically validate the clustering.
How is this even useful instead of simply classifying without clustering?
That is because now that we grouped, we can identify streets with the same features as those with high reported incidence, even if they have no incidents, using the geographic structure to detect risk on streets even if they are under-reported.
Look at the following example over the municipalities of Coyoacán, Benito Juárez, Miguel Hidalgo and Álvaro Obregón, clustered for the years \(2022, 2023, 2024\), based on the logic described above:



Cluster inference for selected areas


From the exploration of crime incidents performed both from qualitative research and from the EDA in Chapter 3, we can see that the clustering for Coyoacán and Álvaro Obregón is very similar to the incidence and security perception of some underdeveloped areas and of high-income, high-security zones. However, for Benito Juárez (BJ) the results seem to be more drastic than what the data says, and this can have two different explanations: one is under-reporting: maybe the model is really telling us where the incidents are occurring and these are not being properly reported. The other is that the model is actually capturing the opportunistic bias, that is, it has identified that connected, high-mobility pedestrian zones are prone to record mugging incidences, and so it classifies a large number of streets in BJ as a Risk level, due to the nature of the municipality itself as a mobility hub for tourist, commercial and experience zones.

title: Embeddings Applications on Crime
text:
Applications: Getting Archetypes
As has been mentioned before, the ideal of modeling crime incidents is not to predict where and in what quantity crime will occur, but to understand the features of the streets —and, in general, of the geometric object of interest— via the embedding features: the features of the streets that are prone to create incentives and opportunity for crime to occur.
Therefore, the idea is that, whether via supervised learning (Regression/Classification) or unsupervised learning (clustering), the streets can be grouped by risk level; this allows, again, not to predict in a literal sense, but to define the high-risk areas, and it opens the door to understanding, with the help of a field specialist, the use cases:

Define security strategies in terms of prioritization or allocation of human capital.
Preventive within-cluster comparison (future): Take high-risk streets and compare the unreported ones of that group; it could be used as surveillance zones where, if not addressed, the incidence could increase.
Preventive within-cluster comparison (diagnostic): Take high-risk streets and compare the unreported ones of that group; in retrospect, it could lead us to find places where crime is being under-reported.
Understand more particular street features with exclusive, high-quality government data: Infrastructure, security camera maintenance, impact of force deployment and causal effect.

Among many other use cases. This shows that, despite not being able to promise a prediction, both modeling approaches give us useful tools to generate valuable insights and actionables.

Risk scoring
Both supervised and unsupervised learning are intermediate tools for our main application of street risk scoring, as an enabler for subsequent decision making, strategy and modeling.
Regression-based risk
Here we use regression models trained for the count process, not to simply predict the incidence level on each street but, particularly when choosing the NN head, we focus on obtaining a probability score per street that allows us to classify each entity into a customized risk level.



Regression based Risk at a city level





Regression based Risk for selected districts


Classification-based risk



Classification based Risk at a city level





Classification based Risk for selected districts




Scoring by clustering
Going back to clustering, we can select some of the high-level streets based on the descriptive statistics of the incidents, and start a deeper study on what is really occurring on those streets, and understand whether it is really a valid signal or just a false positive.



K-Means Clustering adaptation for selected districts and years





K-Means Clustering adaptation for city level and years


Algorithm 1: Assignment of risk levels through clustering
Input: Data matrix X
Output: Risk label ℓ(C_j) for j = 1, …, k*
1:  Fit a clustering model on X; select the optimal number of clusters k*
2:  for j = 1 to k* do
3:      Compute descriptive statistics of cluster C_j
4:      M_j ← max{ incidences within C_j }
5:  end for
6:  j⁻ ← argmin_j M_j          ▷ cluster with lowest statistic of interest
7:  j⁺ ← argmax_j M_j          ▷ cluster with highest statistic of interest
8:  ℓ(C_{j⁻}) ← "low risk"
9:  ℓ(C_{j⁺}) ← "high risk"
10: for all j ∉ {j⁻, j⁺} do
11:     ℓ(C_j) ← "moderate risk"
12: end for
13: return ℓ
Note on well-posedness
Steps 4–5 implicitly assume that argmin_j M_j and argmax_j M_j are each unique. If M_j presents ties at the extremes (plausible if the incidences are integer values and the clusters are small), j⁻ or j⁺ become multivalued and the labeling is not fully specified. A tie-breaking rule is recommended (e.g. lowest cluster index, or largest |C_j|) so that the procedure is deterministic and reproducible.
Some particular modeling and data design decisions that matter:

Most of the risk intervals are defined deterministically; it is important to do this jointly with a field expert to calibrate the thresholds.
The data visualizations have been designed to be neutral in terms of communicating the message of the data, but it is always open to redefinitions and improvements; be careful about how it looks.
The NN architecture, hyperparameters and other training decisions can impact the final results and interpretations.
Zero-inflated count models and data make every model, no matter how optimized, a poor predictor of future counts at the segment (street) level.



Usability and Mock-ups for the data product
As a result, it is proposed to deepen the study of the results obtained from the risk index defined above and, jointly with experts in the area, to evaluate the best model in terms of structural representation of public security risk and, subsequently, to bring the applications proposed below into production.

Crime event monitor
This is a configuration-based Streamlit panel for exploratory data analysis of crime incidents in Mexico City. Data loading, preparation and aggregation are delegated to the source code and wrapped in Streamlit caches, so that the most expensive steps (loading, splitting streets at intersections, spatial joins) run only once. A sidebar shows filters for the year range, crime category, crime type and municipality, and indicates how many incidents have been selected and how many are geolocated.
The following figure shows the start window of the application deployed with the help of the code src/eda/app.py (src/eda/app_esp.py, in Spanish).



Screenshot of the crime activity report Monitoring application




Predictive flagging of risk zones
This is a lightweight, reduced-data-volume interactive presentation of the modeling results. It contains the actual LineString geometry of each street, its name, the predictions, the risk level, the k-means cluster and the PCA coordinates. The design presents two linked side-by-side panels: on the left, a CDMX street map over a Carto Positron basemap in which each street is represented with the color corresponding to its regression risk level (housing risk palette); on the right, a scatter plot in the PCA feature space with points colored according to their spherical k-means k=4 cluster.
The two views are linked to each other through the CVEGEO identifier of each street: when clicking on a street in either panel, the selection is saved in the session state and the application is re-run. It is expected that, if accepted by the stakeholders, the functionalities will grow, allowing their use for the use cases described above as a basis for decision making related to public security based on enriched data.

title: Crime in Mexico
text: One of the most serious social and economic problems is crime. From organized crime to financial fraud, Mexico faces in its modern history a series of challenges in matters of crime and security. On the other hand, Mexico and its institutions, such as INEGI, have very high-quality open data and information, particularly for Mexico City. Thus, it is a good candidate for carrying out an interesting exercise on crime incidence and earth embeddings.

title: Crime in Mexico
text:
Context and phenomenon
Crime and public insecurity consistently rank among the main concerns of the Mexican population. According to INEGI’s National Survey of Victimization and Perception of Public Security (ENVIPE), an estimated 23.1 million people aged 18 or older were victims of some crime during 2024 —a rate of approximately 24,135 victims per 100,000 inhabitants— and the economic cost of crime and insecurity reached about 269.6 billion pesos, close to 1.07% of GDP [INEGI, ENVIPE 2025].
A structural feature of the phenomenon is under-reporting. ENVIPE estimates that, of the approximately 33.5 million crimes committed in 2024, only a small fraction was reported and formally investigated, so that the cifra negra —the proportion of crimes neither reported nor investigated— stands at around 93% [INEGI, ENVIPE 2025]. This gap is central to any data-based analysis: administrative records such as the carpetas de investigación used in this work capture only the visible tip of the distribution, not the phenomenon itself.
The perception of insecurity is equally high and spatially heterogeneous. In the third quarter of 2025, about 63% of the adult population in the 91 urban areas surveyed by INEGI’s National Urban Public Security Survey (ENSU) considered it unsafe to live in their city, with public spaces —ATMs, public transport and the street— perceived as the least safe [INEGI, ENSU 2025]. Mexico City concentrates this contrast sharply: boroughs such as Benito Juárez report some of the lowest perceptions of insecurity in the country, while others rank well above the national average, which underscores that insecurity in the capital is a fundamentally local, sub-city-level phenomenon —precisely the granularity this work seeks.

title: Crime in Mexico
section: Crime incidence in Mexico City (CDMX) - Available data
text:
Crime incidence in Mexico City (CDMX) - Available data
One of the most relevant problems in matters of crime in Mexico, both for measuring the state of the situation and for public policy creation, is the quantity, quality and reliability of crime data at the national level, which makes the idea of making data-based anti-crime strategy decisions a distant dream. The main concerns are:

Censored data records (unreported, corrupted) due to the population’s fear and to corruption.
Bureaucratic barriers and legacy data management systems and processes.
Low incentives to improve or increase data collection and transparency processes.

However, given the global relevance and the growing presence of global citizens and investments in Mexico City, data transparency portals such as the Sistema Ajolote de Datos Abiertos CDMX have been providing data that is good enough to generate analyses and reports on crime incidence throughout the city, at a granularity level that reaches lat/lon precision (with the exception of records that constitute a risk for the victims).
This gives a good starting point to begin a more precise assessment of crime incidence in the city.

FGJ’s Carpetas de Investigación
One of the most important datasets is ‘Carpetas de Investigación’ —the case files opened by Mexico City’s Fiscalía General de Justicia (FGJ). We can download the data directly from the portal with the following code:
# Direct download for Carpetas de Investigacion
# Up to 2025-01
 wget https://archivo.datos.cdmx.gob.mx/FGJ/carpetas/carpetasFGJ_acumulado_2025_01.csv -O ./data/raw/carpetasFGJ.csv --no-check-certificate
Consider that it is important to add --no-check-certificate, because, despite being the official site, the page’s certificate is sometimes expired.

Data Assessment for Carpetas de Investigación
