2. Low-information / redundant fields

municipio_hecho — single value CDMX for all 2.1M rows. No analytical value.
alcaldia_catalogo — a single non-null value and 99.2% missing values. Drop.
competencia — half empty; treat absence as “unspecified”, not as a class.
colonia_catalogo vs colonia_hecho and alcaldia_catalogo vs alcaldia_hecho are catalog/free-text twins; the _hecho variants are far more complete and should be the canonical fields.

3. Duplicates
Source: dq_duplicates.csv.

Exact duplicates (all 21 columns identical): 4,735 rows (0.226%).
Incident-key duplicates (same fecha_hecho, hora_hecho, delito, latitud, longitud, colonia_hecho, alcaldia_hecho): 11,432 rows (0.545%).

The gap between the two means that ~6,700 records describe the same event/place but differ in administrative metadata (agency, unit). Deduplicate on the incident key for crime counting; keep all rows for caseload analysis.



C5 citizen reports
The “C5”, which comes from its full name “Centro de Comando, Control, Cómputo, Comunicaciones y Contacto Ciudadano de la Ciudad de México” (Mexico City Command, Control, Computing, Communications, and Citizen Contact Center), is a huge system that collects, via thousands of cameras, emergency buttons and contact centers, a large amount of citizen reports, some of which are false or merely informative; however, it provides a rich source of criminal and non-criminal reports throughout the city’s streets. To learn more about it, consider checking the C5 Official Website.
To access the most up-to-date 3-year version of the report collection, run:
 # C5 Direct download 
wget https://archivo.datos.cdmx.gob.mx/C5/incidentes_viales/inViales_2022_2024.csv -O ./data/raw/c5_reports.csv --no-check-certificate
Also, consider that it is important to add --no-check-certificate, because, despite being the official site, the page’s certificate is sometimes expired.
In this work we will lean toward the first dataset, but we encourage readers to repeat the exercise with this second dataset, not with crime incidences but with emergency calls.


Basic EDA on CDMX crime incidents
The following statistics were obtained from the ‘Carpetas de Investigación’ from 2016 up to January 2025, using only the records with complete data in the columns: ["delito", "categoria_delito", "mes_inicio", "agencia", "municipio_hecho", "anio_inicio", "mes_hecho", "anio_hecho", "fecha_inicio", "hora_hecho", "fecha_hecho", "latitud", "longitud"].
We can see that, of the 15 most committed crimes in CDMX, the most represented are “Violencia Familiar” (domestic violence) and “Fraude” (fraud), followed by multiple types of “Robo” (theft), which supports the idea that crimes in Mexico City have a strong materialistic and socioeconomic motivation.



Top 15 crimes


When we group the crimes into categories, we can see that robbery of individuals and car theft remain the main occurrences.



Top crimes by category


We can see that the monthly crime trend, despite having decreased in recent years, remains at constant levels after the COVID-19 pandemic.



Monthly Trend





YoY Changes


When analyzing incidents by hour and day, we can observe, from the following figures, that most occurrences happen during working hours. This could be a natural distribution, but also, when focusing on the hourly detail, it is clear that an administrative bias exists, due to the processing of the reports:



Day and hour occurences





Hour distribution


However, when decomposing by the crime itself we can see some patterns in the occurrence of particular crimes throughout the day:



Hour crimes per category


Particularly, for the interest of this report, it is important to understand the spatial patterns in the data.



Spatial distribution (by KDE on coordinates)


As we can see, there is a concentration of crimes in the center of the city, which can be explained by the total population present in the region. More detailed per capita analytics will be presented later to clarify the concentration of the incidence in a spatial sense.


A closer look at some crimes
Let us consider some of the most relevant crime categories and use them as an example of a spatial analysis across multiple geometry types; in this case we are taking a closer look at: homicide, street robbery and home burglary.
First we create a series of auxiliary databases:

## Import libraries 
import pandas as pd
import geopandas as gpd 

## Read full data set 
df = pd.read_csv("./data/clean/carpetasFGJ.csv").query("year >= 2016")

## Save filtered data

# Murder 
df.query(" crime_cat == 'HOMICIDIO DOLOSO' ").to_csv("./data/clean/carpetasFGJ_homicidios.csv", index = False)

# Street robbery 
df.query(" crime_cat == 'ROBO A TRANSEUNTE EN VÍA PÚBLICA CON Y SIN VIOLENCIA' ").to_csv("./data/clean/carpetasFGJ_asaltos.csv", index = False)

# House robbery
df.query(" crime_cat == 'ROBO A CASA HABITACIÓN CON VIOLENCIA' ").to_csv("./data/clean/carpetasFGJ_robo.csv", index = False)


A deep look at mugging incidents (Asalto a transeúnte)
Now, let us take a deep look at a particular crime that is not only one of the most observed in the database, but also, because of its structural definition, will force us to understand the nature of its geometry: that is mugging (Robo a Transeúnte con y sin violencia, in its Spanish denomination).
The monthly trend of mugging had a relevant peak in 2019, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, and since then has kept a stable incidence across time, particularly from 2022 to 2024, the candidate years for a deeper analysis.



Monthly patterns for mugging in CDMX


Consider the following day-of-week and month-level rhythms, and also the hourly cadence for reported mugging in CDMX. As we can see, it is clear that the most frequent moments are on weekdays and at dinner times and the typical end of the working day, which indicates that this crime is highly opportunistic, that is, it tends to occur depending on the flow of transit.



Day and month cadence for mugging





Hourly rhythm


A first spatial analysis to understand is the direct location in space of the crime event. As observed in the figure below, despite being distributed throughout the whole populated area of the city, there are clear patterns that resemble some accumulation or grouping of the points into hotspots.



Crime ocurrences by year


In order to evaluate the apparent grouping, we apply a DBSCAN, an unsupervised algorithm designed to identify the spatial grouping of points, given some proximity parameter and a minimum cluster size, based both on the number of points and on their proximity.



DBSCAN yearly pattern for particular crime


As we can see, we confirm that for each year clusters form in contrast with the identified noise. This supports the thesis that crime apparently tends to cluster across space for each year.
Despite the positive results, there are some particular criticisms of this approach, namely that, even under DBSCAN’s assumption, incidence is assumed to be continuous across space, when in reality crime is bounded by geographic space, which is discrete, non-uniform and designed by humans, and dynamically changed by societies; this is why, from a serious analysis, it is important to keep the correct geographic referencing.
For example, for this particular crime that by definition occurs on the street, the correct referencing and aggregation level must be at the street level.
See the figure below, where crime events are aggregated at the street level (corner to corner) by year.



Street frequency by year


Now we can see that, even without being continuous, the spatial patterns hold, supporting the thesis that crime is not constant across urban space.

title: Working with Embeddings
text:
Working with Vector Embeddings
Regardless of the model used for the embeddings, there are some properties we would like to see in this feature, some of which are described below.

Similarity between entities
The notion of similarity over embeddings could be misunderstood if we do not remember what they are, that is, a collection of vectors from a latent space, and thus the similarity of the representations can be evaluated in terms of vector similarity.
In general, one of the most relevant similarity metrics is Cosine Similarity, defined below.
Def. The cosine similarity between two vectors \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{\mathbf{0}\}\) is defined as:
\[ S_c(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \cos(\theta) = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|_2 \, \|\mathbf{v}\|_2} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} u_i v_i}{\sqrt{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} u_i^2} \cdot \sqrt{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} v_i^2}}\]
where \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) is the angle subtended by \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) in the inner-product space, and \(\|\cdot\|_2\) denotes the Euclidean (\(L^2\)) norm. This is a direct consequence of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, which guarantees \(\cos(\theta) \in [-1, 1]\).
More generally, in any real inner-product space \((\mathcal{H}, \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle)\):
\[ \cos(\theta) = \frac{\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle}{\|\mathbf{u}\| \, \|\mathbf{v}\|}\]
It is important to note that cosine similarity is not properly a metric in the sense of the metrics induced on metric or Hilbert spaces; however, its use in different statistical learning methods and its meaning as “proximity” between vectors make it a suitable value for evaluating the similarity between vector representations of entities (embeddings).
Considering this, we can define the cosine distance for unit vectors as:
\[
D_c(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) = \operatorname{dist}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \sqrt{(\mathbf{u}- \mathbf{v}) \cdot (\mathbf{u}- \mathbf{v})} = \sqrt{2(1-S_c(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}))}
\]
and sometimes also known or defined as:
\[
D_c(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) = 1 - S_c(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})
\]
In the end, the intent of Cosine Similarity is that similar places at the same moment (point coordinates at a given time) based on their features should have similar values representing them as entities, that is, despite spatial distance, political divisions and geographic separations, similar places should be similar in the feature space defined by the embedding.
For this task we performed a small experiment using the 64-dimensional feature space created by Google Earth Embedding V1 to analyze the similarity between 8 different residential areas of the Mexico City Metropolitan Area shown in the following figure:



Selected points in the Mexico City metropolitan area

We can see the similarities in the following heatmap:



Cosine Similarity heatmap for the selected POIs


Despite observing notable differences between points with different socio-demographic characteristics, the metric does not fully differentiate the structural features, and given that all points are from a broadly similar region, the cosine similarity stays close to one in most cases.
Therefore, we can apply a PCA analysis to use the variance between points as a way of differentiating the nature of the selected points.
After reprojecting each point vector onto the 2 components of the PCA(k=2) decomposition, we explore their position on the new PC1-PC2 plane.



POIs projected onto PC1 and PC2


Now, in the decomposition, we can see that similar places, such as ‘Condesa’ and ‘Lomas’ or ‘Ciudad Neza’ and ‘Santo Domingo’, end up closer to each other, and we can also observe a separation of the points into sections; we can then interpret the meaning of the index values using socio-demographic and empirical knowledge. Take for example the following:

PC1: Represents low-income areas; the lower the index, the higher the expected income.
PC2: Could be associated with ‘Purely Residential’: the lower the index, the higher the probability of being on mixed-use land (commercial, industrial and residential).

Despite being a basic interpretation, and requiring many more data points to improve the indices derived from the components, this small exercise shows us the potential of these embedding vectors to understand, describe and identify latent features of geographic points through purely numerical features, and to translate it into actionable information.
The code and step-by-step logic of the material covered in the next section can be consulted in the Local Similarity Variance Notebook.
For example, let us take a region (area) of interest (AoI) from which to extract embeddings; in this case, we select the Coyoacán Borough (Alcaldía) within Mexico City. The official political division and the SHP files can be found at Mexico’s INEGI Official Web Page.
The selected area shown below (Coyoacán, Mexico City) is useful for this analysis because it has the following properties that make the analysis homogeneous (relatively ‘square’ covered area, diversity of urban patterns, coexistence of multiple socioeconomic levels, and contained POIs such as parks or stadiums).



Visualization of our AoI




Limits of Cosine Similarity
Cosine similarity, or its corresponding proper metric function, cosine distance or angular distance, is one of the strongest functions in Data Science for understanding similarity in high dimensions, and particularly when working with embeddings. Because the implicit assumption for embeddings is that they are already processed features of the object of interest, cosine similarity turns out to be a critical tool for finding patterns between pairs of points.
For this exercise, we take a point (\((-99.17095, 19.35364)\)) in the middle of Viveros de Coyoacán, a well-known conservation park in Mexico City, and pair it with the corresponding features of the \(10m\) cell as a reference vector. Then all the corresponding points where the cosine similarity is above a threshold in \([0.80, 0.95]\) were plotted.



Green mass detection via Cosine Similarity thresholding


As we can see, by just taking an embedding of a well-known pixel representing the object of interest, in this case a tree, we can recover a large amount of green mass (other trees or vegetation), simply by relaxing the similarity threshold enough to recognize, but not so low as to contaminate with false positives.
This says a lot about the large amount of abstraction and the particular embedded details of the objects captured via the vector embeddings.
The same exercise can be repeated with water bodies, obtaining even better results.


Latent features of Embeddings
One of the assumptions —moreover, more than an assumption, it is actually part of the nature of embeddings by training design— is that we seek to embed latent features of the generating process from which the data come, and that lives in multidimensional geometric objects. Thus, when working with embeddings or vector bases, a good first instinct is to use dimensionality reduction techniques to understand or visualize the nature of the data we have at hand.



Embedding Dimensionality Reduction Methods over AlphaEarth 2023


Methods such as PCA allow us to evaluate the characteristics of the features in low-dimensional forms while keeping as much of the data as possible (amount of variance of the total), and in combination with clustering methods such as K-means they allow us to visualize the grouping patterns of multidimensional features.
The t-SNE algorithm applies a non-linear dimensionality reduction to identify the distributionally similar features of the points.

title: Working with Embeddings
text:
Applications of embeddings
The nature of embeddings is so rich in terms of contained information because these features come from large volumes of data processed in a supervised algorithm for multiple tasks, which allows the models to capture multiple domain-specific features and meaning embedded throughout the features in the defined latent space. However, this strength is also its weakness when it comes to applying and modeling using embeddings, and it is even harder when these applications go beyond a theoretical space and enter a cross-domain application; because of the generality and sparsity of embeddings, it is important to correctly define the scope and architecture of the model, as well as the success metrics beyond the performance metrics for the chosen model or algorithm.
In addition, most of the time in a local setting (city or district level), even the most distinct regions can be really similar in terms of cosine similarity or any other similarity metric. (See the Low variance in local settings section below.)
Despite these drawbacks, there are many techniques that can help us exploit the value of embeddings in multiple applications; here are some techniques and models.

Plug-and-play model patterns for embeddings
The following are some techniques used when working with embeddings; these examples are far from exhaustive, and the field is currently growing and defining new model frameworks and techniques; consider also that the list intends to cover the general applications and objectives in machine learning, such as predicting, estimating, classifying or revealing patterns in the data. More complex or special-purpose use cases could use more sophisticated tools and models, or even frontier development.
Based on Cosine Similarity
It might be repetitive, but the use of cosine similarity over numerical vectors is a powerful tool for identifying groups and giving semantic meaning to a topic, even more so when working with spherical data (such as AlphaEarth Embeddings).
Some direct applications are:

Look-a-Likes: Given an identified target, search all the similar entities with respect to the object of interest.
Networking applications: Based on similarity, define entities as nodes and connect them according to similarity thresholds. Enabling all planar graph models, at least.
Direct clustering: Basis for all clustering algorithms that use it as a distance function (using the appropriate distance metric definition).

This technique is basic because it is the basis of most models and metrics, and also because of its direct use given a vector base.
Dimensionality Reduction
For some cases such as Earth Embeddings, the amount of available features can sometimes add noise instead of a clear signal; that is when Dimensionality Reduction, just like cosine similarity, appears both as a preprocessing step and as a method to understand the global properties of the embeddings in fewer dimensions, for visualization and to obtain more interpretable features, such as PCA or t-SNE. (See multiple applications throughout all the pages of this work.)
Naive Regression
A first attempt at using embedding features in supervised learning is to take a direct approach and try to fit or model a linear relationship (or even Generalized Linear Models) on a target variable \(y\) in terms of the embedding features:
\[ y \sim E^t\beta + \epsilon\]
Where \(E\) is the embedding vector, and \(\epsilon\) a random variable.
We call this approach naive not because it is inherently incorrect or wrong (it is in fact used in this work), but because since embeddings contain a large amount of data, this can induce variance in the model, which makes it difficult to study with traditional methods and rarely leads to an interpretable and statistically significant result at the same time.
Regression Covariates
Another way to use embeddings as a feature in a linear regression is to use them, particularly a low-dimensional projection, not only as the sole variables but as a data enrichment to a current set of regressor variables, particularly if this one is not geographic in nature.
Using the following structure:
\[ y \sim X^t\beta_x + E_d^t\beta_e + \epsilon\]
Where \(E_d\) is an embedding vector projected onto a \(d\)-dimensional space, \(X\) are the related features, and \(\epsilon\) a random variable.
As we have mentioned before, the amount of data in the embeddings can add additional variance, particularly in a linear model, so the use of a low-dimensional projection is the middle ground for extracting as much important data as possible without adding a large amount of variance to the model.
Classification
Following the same logic as regression, when the target \(y\) is categorical, in our case a binary indicator of whether an event occurred or not, we can fit a classifier over the embedding features, alone or combined with other regressor variables:
\[ P(y=1 \mid E, X) = \sigma\left(X^t\beta_x + E_d^t\beta_e\right)\]
Where \(\sigma\) is the sigmoid link function. The same caveats about the variance added by embeddings apply here, and so does the benefit of using them either as the sole predictor or as an enrichment layer over the structural covariates, particularly useful given that event-based targets tend to be highly imbalanced.
Neural Network Heads (NN Heads)
A further extension over the linear (or generalized linear) plug-in models above is to replace the linear combination \(\beta\), both for regression and classification, with a small neural network —a head— trained over the (fixed) embedding vector. That is, instead of \(E^t\beta\) we learn a function \(g_\theta(E)\), typically a shallow Multilayer Perceptron, which directly produces the parameter of interest (a count mean, a class logit).
This allows the model to capture non-linear interactions between the embedding dimensions that a simple regression cannot, at the cost of losing the direct interpretability of each coefficient \(\beta\), and demanding more data and regularization care to avoid overfitting, given that embeddings are already a dense, information-rich feature space.
And on top of each of these models we can go on to improve them and make them more complex; think, for example, of not only using and training an output layer, but of using a more sophisticated technique such as an attention mechanism.


Real-world applications
Weather prediction and improvement
Since Earth Embeddings such as AlphaEarth already assimilate climate reanalysis and atmospheric layers among their training sources, they can serve as compact covariates for short-term meteorological nowcasting, or for correcting the bias of low-resolution reanalysis products down to a hyperlocal resolution, without needing to stand up a full physical simulation model.
Disaster Risk Scoring
The same archetype explored throughout this work, scoring streets by crime risk, extends directly to natural hazards such as floods, landslides or wildfires: use the embeddings as a proxy for terrain, vegetation and infrastructure features, and then apply the same supervised or unsupervised patterns described above to flag high-risk areas, even where the historical record of the hazard is incomplete.
Real estate valuation enrichment
Hedonic pricing models for real estate traditionally rely on structural property features (surface area, rooms, age), leaving aside the neighborhood and environmental features that are hard to hand-code. Embeddings can enrich these models as an additional regressor variable, capturing latent information about amenities, accessibility and land use around the property, in the same spirit as the socioeconomic data enrichment used throughout this work.
Agriculture and climate change
The systemic shock technique described above, comparing the embedding of the same point across time via cosine similarity, applies directly to land-use change relevant to agriculture and climate monitoring, such as deforestation, crop rotation or drought stress, without needing a bespoke model for each phenomenon of interest.

title: Working with Embeddings
text:
Caveats when working with embeddings
As can be seen in the previous section, embeddings, when decomposed (via dimensionality reduction) with methods such as PCA, can be informative about the nature and similarity of different points in a similar region in terms of infrastructure, socioeconomic level and urban design, but if we pay attention to the similarity heatmap, even the most dissimilar points have a similarity around 0.7 (more similar than not). That is why it is important to understand the local variability of embeddings. Because embeddings are derived from training a ViT on Earth-level models, most of the data at the local level is shared (temperature, vegetation, distance to the tropics, climate and weather, within the same political division); this is why we want to understand, at the local level (under similar conditions), how the embeddings differ.

Low variance in local settings
For example, if we take the 64 embedding vectors for the selected region. To do so, we run EE Embeddings from an AoI and extract data for a raster at the 10m level, to understand how different the vectors are at neighborhood scale:



First 3 vector values for the embeddings in Coyoacán


As we can see, the patterns of each band are similar and the differences are hard to identify at first inspection, and given that, as we mentioned before, the embedding vectors carry an enormous amount of local features, we must perform a dimensionality reduction.
For this part of the exercise we performed a PCA decomposition using k=7, which accounts for up to 75% of the variance, obtaining the following results:
.
In the first component \(PC1\) we can see blurry but grouped areas, which account for what we can interpret as ‘shared regional features’.
In \(PC2\) and \(PC6\) we can clearly see a pattern that defines roads and streets, which allows us to interpret these components as indicators of buildings/infrastructure compared to roads and streets.
\(PC3\) and \(PC4\), for example, have more uniformly distributed values, being the components that carry the regional features.
In contrast, when we look at \(PC5\), we can clearly see defined regions where the values vary based on some patterns; given the existing knowledge, it seems to classify between green areas vs. built infrastructure.
Taking this last point as a piece of evidence to defend the thesis that Earth Embeddings, despite including world-level data in latent dimensions, also include granular information about particular POIs or infrastructure.
Analyzing embeddings at a \(10m\) granularity and at the district level is almost intractable in terms of benchmarking and comparing differences, given the number of pairwise combinations to compare (\(\binom{N}{2}\) with \(N > 500k\)).
In addition, if we use the official geographic divisions to evaluate the consistency of the embeddings across the official political-urban divisions, let us work on a neighborhood-level (colonia) comparison.
To understand how the vector values are assigned to each neighborhood, street, or in general to polygons, see the Working with Aggregation Levels section.
Benchmark computation

We take the pixel coverage, that is, the 10m raster, (see image below) of the polygon.
We compute the pairwise cosine similarity for each pixel vector (where each entry is a band for the given pixel) for each pixel of the coverage, for each neighborhood level (MZA-CVEGEO for the present case, check Mexico INEGI’s Marco Geoestadístico).
We compute the aggregate (mean/median) for the metrics computed in each CVEGEO.

In the following chart, we see the similarity distributions:



Cosine Similarity distributions for CVEGEO within the embeddings


From this, we can take the assumption that the mean/median aggregation of the pixel coverage preserves the embedding representations at the local level.
In addition, it is important to consider that, apparently, the within similarity is uniform across the area of interest at the local level.



Mean Cosine Similarity for within embeddings


Let us switch to an even larger administrative area, to see how well the similarity between the within embeddings holds by sections.



Within cosine similarity heatmap at AGEB Level (mean aggregation)


In the figure we can see that the well-known barrios (unofficial local neighborhoods) have a high similarity score, and the low-similarity areas correspond to mixed-use areas such as UNAM’s Ciudad Universitaria, which is the National University campus, including buildings, parks, forest reserves, laboratories and various natural and infrastructure sites.
Now, for the AGEB (group of MZAs), let us look at the sampled similarity:



Within cosine similarity at AGEB Level (mean aggregation)


Here the mean and the median seem to have different distributions across the regions, and this is why it is important to think more deeply about the selection of the aggregation metric.
In general, what we can see is that the vector values are similar at the CVEGEO level for both the MZA and AGEB aggregation levels, but as is evident on the map, streets are not included, particularly for the MZA case, even though the embeddings cover them completely; so let us repeat the exercise under the same logic but taking the corresponding streets.



Street-level cosine similarity


From here we can see that most streets are more similar than not in general, but the actual geometries can be hard to interpret; so it is important to obtain the sampled similarity over each geometry throughout the region.



Street-level cosine similarity


Despite the bimodal behavior of the similarity, we can still conclude that most units maintain a high degree of similarity among themselves.


Systemic shocks in the embedding representation
Another feature of vector embeddings, particularly with AlphaEarth, is that they not only offer full coverage of the Earth’s surface, but also perform a training of the whole model with an annual cadence.
We can then study systemic shocks, which in this context means radical changes in surface patterns that are reflected in the embedding representations.
To do so, we take the Ceteris paribus approach, that is, given a series of embeddings over \((lat,lon,time)\), over a fixed point on Earth, what is the difference of the embedding along the temporal dimension?, this measured via cosine similarity.
Here is the distribution for all pairwise cosine similarities of all embeddings within our AoI (Coyoacán):



Cosine similarity between years for the AoI


And here the pixel points at which the similarity of the corresponding embedding vector between the years 2022 and 2023 is at most \(0.85\).



Points with cosine similarity below 0.85


Digging deeper into the nature of the points where we identified important changes, we can see the following example



Example of a shock in detail


As we can see in the figure, at the points where the embeddings show low similarity, we identify that a building was constructed on an empty lot during the year 2022. This shows the simple but powerful methodology for identifying important geographic changes on the ground, enabled by the use of embeddings.


Working with Aggregation Levels
As shown before, each model has its own logic and aggregation, and we can find the following 2 types of embeddings:

Discrete: Found mainly in the form of rasters (square grids covering an area of interest), or any other discrete (countably finite) set of political, geographic or geometric division (H3, square cells). Given this, despite the complex differences and trade-offs between them, for the purpose of this section they are seen as the same thing: a discrete division of the space of interest, that is, a finite disjoint partition of the space into polygonal objects.
Continuous: Continuous representation of space, either on a plane (2D/3D Euclidean) or any continuous projection (spherical, cylindrical) over non-Euclidean geometries. In addition, for simplicity, we can see this as coordinates (a tuple of values representing a position).

Beyond the geometry type of the data structure, what really defines the type of aggregation is the way the event is represented in general. Let us think about the representation of the Earth’s surface: if we use a coordinate system, that is, a (lat, lon) tuple, with an infinite (in theory) number of possible points between any pair of points. In contrast, if we use Uber’s H3 partition, given any two cells, or even two points, there is a finite number of resolution-\(r\) H3 cells between them.
Let us work with our Alpha Earth raster embeddings to explain the aggregation logic:
Polygon Assignment
Suppose we want to assign the vector values from our \(10m\) raster, and that we want to assign those raster values to a given polygon whose extent is larger than a single cell; the accepted way to do this is via the aggregation of its raster coverage, as seen in the following figure:



Pixel coverage logic for Political Division


That is, given a polygon, we use the raster coverage of that polygon (each cell that touches the polygon’s area) and then take the mean vector value of all those raster cells, and finally normalize it, this in order to be consistent with AlphaEarth Embeddings and most embedding bases, which are normalized, and particularly with the AlphaEarth base, keeping the aggregated result in the \(S^{63}\) space as described in the official documentation.
Linestring Aggregation
This logic stays the same regardless of the geometry of the object of interest; see, for example, the following example for a street segment:



Pixel coverage of a street segment


Most of the problems when working with either of the two types are due to not using a correct standard and unified projection and to not using the correct aggregation and geometric entities. For more detail on how to work with geographic data, see the Geospatial Data Appendix.
As we have seen, despite not having (in theory) area, the logic holds: select all the cells touched by the object, and then repeat the normalization step of the aggregation.

title: Earth Embeddings
text:
It is not hard to define what embeddings are; the hard part is understanding how to create an embedding and how to benchmark which ones are actually useful or informative for the entities or fields they intend to represent.
Def (Embedding): In the context of mathematics and machine learning, we define an embedding \(x_i \in X\) of the object \(i \subset A\) as a vector representation of the object \(i\) where \(X \subset \mathbb{R}^n\), defined via a relation \(f\) such that: \(f:A \rightarrow X\).
The convention is that \(x_i\) is an embedding vector representing the object \(i\) of the (finite or infinite) set \(A\), while \(X\) is the embedding base (space) representing the set \(A\) itself. In the literature, and particularly in this content, embedding will be used for both depending on context, specifying only when disambiguation is required.
Some implicit expectations about embeddings —implicit since it is the goal for an embedding to satisfy them, even though they are not necessarily met in the process of generating embeddings— are the following:

The embedding base (\(X\)) must be derived exclusively from the data universe \(A\).
To each element \(a_i\) there corresponds a unique vector \(x_i\).
The minimal spanning vector space for \(X\) must keep the meaning of \(A\) embedded in the geometry of that vector space.



The need for embeddings arises naturally in the practice of machine learning and statistical modeling. When working with tabular datasets, there are instances in which, in order to understand and model phenomena, we use feature engineering, creating a series of derived metrics. Other times the object we study is really hard to handle —for example text, images or physical objects— due to their finite but almost unmanageable quantities and combinations of objects, or because of their continuous and complex behavior; then creating models of the reality those objects represent is difficult. For those cases there is the option of creating embeddings, that is, taking some set and, via a process \(f\) (some of which are discussed below), representing it in vector form, a very well known, computable and studied mathematical object.
The following figure describes the general process for the generation of embedding bases, where the model can range from simple assignment rules, hash functions or feature engineering, to outputs of complex neural networks or weights between layers.



Embedding generation process


For a more visual explanation of what we expect from a (good) embedding, let us look at the following figure. On the left we have the existence of embedding dimensions, in which we expect to see words group together based on their semantic meaning. That translates into a geometric sense, in which similar objects (in this example, text) keep a sense of geometric similarity: similar objects are sent to similar embeddings.



Illustrative characterization of embedding vectors.





Following the logic already outlined, text is perhaps the canonical object that resists naive modeling. A corpus is a discrete set whose atoms —words, subwords, sentences— have a finite inventory, but they combine into an effectively unlimited space of possibilities; and, worse still, the meaning we care about does not live in the symbols themselves but in the company they keep. This is the old distributional intuition, isolated by Harris and memorably formulated by Firth: a word is characterized by the words that surround it [Harris 1954; Firth 1957]. A text embedding is then a mapping
\[f : V \to \mathbb{R}^{d} \]
over the token vocabulary \(V\) (or \(f:\Sigma^{*} \to \mathbb{R}^{d}\) over spans) that turns these purely relational and combinatorial objects into vectors over which geometry becomes semantics —cosine proximity approximating the degree of relatedness and, famously, vector translations approximating analogies. The first generation learned a single static vector per word from co-occurrence statistics: word2vec optimizes a self-supervised objective —predict the context from the center word, or the other way around— whose optimum places words with similar distributions close together [Mikolov et al. 2013], while GloVe reaches a comparable geometry by factorizing a global co-occurrence matrix [Pennington et al. 2014]. However, such a static \(f\) cannot separate the two senses of bank. The second generation therefore made the embedding contextual, letting \(f\) depend on the full sentence, so that the same token receives different vectors in different contexts —the move industrialized by BERT [Devlin et al. 2019] and extended to complete passages, for retrieval and clustering, by sentence-level encoders such as Sentence-BERT [Reimers & Gurevych 2019]. The gain is exactly the one promised in the general case: an intractable relational object is replaced by points in a well known, computable and exhaustively studied space.



The previous examples take the embedding as the final product; the variational autoencoder is worth studying because it inverts the emphasis and treats the embedding as a latent cause. Suppose we posit that each observed datum \(x\) is generated from an unobserved code \(z\), drawn from a simple prior \(p(z)\) —conventionally a standard Gaussian— and transformed through a decoder \(p_{\theta}(x \mid z)\). Embedding \(x\) now consists of inferring its posterior \(p(z \mid x)\), the distribution over codes that could have produced it; but this posterior is intractable for any interesting decoder. Kingma and Welling’s resolution is to approximate it with an encoder \(q_{\phi}(z \mid x)\) and to train encoder and decoder jointly by maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO) [Kingma & Welling 2014; Rezende et al. 2014]:
\[ \log p_{\theta}(x) \ge \mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;x) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z\mid x)}\!\left[\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z)\right]}_{\text{reconstruction}} - \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\!\left(q_{\phi}(z\mid x)\,\Vert\,p(z)\right)}_{\text{regularization}}. \]
The two terms read as an instruction and a discipline: reconstruct \(x\) faithfully, but keep the code distribution close to the prior, so that the latent space remains smooth and samplable instead of degenerating into a lookup table. The only technical obstacle —that we must backpropagate through a sampling step— is removed with the reparameterization trick, writing \(z = \mu_{\phi}(x) + \sigma_{\phi}(x)\odot\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\), which pushes the randomness into a variable independent of the input and restores a differentiable path. What we obtain, then, is not merely a vector per object, but an embedding space endowed with a probabilistic grammar: a continuous, low-dimensional manifold along which we can interpolate and from which we can sample —the same well-behaved vector goal as before, now equipped with a generative explanation of how the objects arose.



General VAE framework (By EugenioTL - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=107231101)





If the VAE provides a probabilistic reason to want good embeddings, the Transformer provides the mechanism that computes the best ones we currently have. Its starting point is, once again, a limitation of previous tools: recurrent and convolutional encoders build context locally and sequentially, so that dependencies between distant elements are mediated through long chains and are consequently expensive to learn. The Transformer discards recurrence and lets each element attend directly to all the others through self-attention [Vaswani et al. 2017]. Concretely, from an input matrix \(X\) queries, keys and values are formed via linear mappings, \(Q = X W_{Q}\), \(K = X W_{K}\), \(V = X W_{V}\), and are mixed through
\[ \mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V)\;=\;\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right) V , \]
so that each output vector is a data-dependent weighted average of all the others —a content-addressed retrieval in which the weights are learned similarities and the factor \(\sqrt{d_{k}}\) simply keeps the logits on a suitable scale. Several of these mappings run in parallel (multi-head attention) to capture different relational patterns at once; and since the operation is permutation-equivariant, order must be reinjected through positional encodings. The result is precisely a machine for contextual embedding: it consumes a set (or sequence) of vectors and returns a set of the same shape in which each one has been rewritten in terms of its relevant neighbors. This is why the architecture underpins the contextual text embeddings above; this is why —with images cut into patches and treated as tokens— it gives rise to the Vision Transformer [Dosovitskiy et al. 2021]; and this is why, combined with a masked reconstruction objective in the style of the masked autoencoder [He et al. 2022], it has become the default engine for learning representations of almost any object we can serialize into tokens.



Base architecture of a Vision Transformer (By Davide Coccomini - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=110678226)





Which brings us to the hardest object on the list. The Earth’s surface is neither a finite vocabulary nor a tidy image; it is a continuous, four-dimensional field, observed only indirectly, through a heterogeneous fleet of instruments. Sometimes we see it in optical and thermal bands (Sentinel-2, Landsat); other times through cloud-penetrating radar (Sentinel-1 SAR), laser altimetry of vegetation structure (GEDI, LiDAR), reanalysis climate variables (ERA5-Land), or even the planet’s gravitational field (GRACE) —each with its own resolution, cadence and noise regime, and each riddled with gaps left by clouds, orbit and revisit time. The modeling difficulty is then of a different kind than that of text: not the combinatorics of a discrete set, but the fusion of many partial, continuous and poorly registered views of an evolving system —compounded by the scarcity that dominates the field, namely petabytes of pixels against very few labels, because a single ground-truth datum means that someone physically visited a place at a given time [Jakubik et al. 2023; Brown et al. 2025]. The natural answer has been to import the machinery just described wholesale: treat stacks of satellite imagery as cubes of spatiotemporal tokens, pre-train a Vision-Transformer encoder through masked reconstruction, and thereby learn a general representation of the surface without labels —the strategy of geospatial foundation models such as Prithvi, pre-trained self-supervised on the harmonized Landsat–Sentinel archive and then fine-tuned for flood mapping, crop segmentation and the like [Jakubik et al. 2023; Szwarcman et al. 2024]. The object is monstrous, but the recipe is the familiar one: find a mapping \(f\) into a computable vector space.
The culmination is to take the embedding idea to its literal extreme and vectorize the planet itself: assign to each place, and to each year, a compact code that summarizes everything the instruments, taken together, say about it. Two complementary readings of “Earth embedding” have emerged. In the first, the location is embedded: SatCLIP learns a location encoder by contrastively aligning geographic coordinates —lifted to the sphere through spherical-harmonic positional features— with the satellite imagery observed at that place, producing a lightweight \(f : (\mathrm{lat}, \mathrm{lon}) \to \mathbb{R}^{d}\) whose vectors already predict temperature, population density or species presence at a point [Klemmer et al. 2025]. In the second, more encompassing reading, the surface field itself is embedded directly: AlphaEarth Foundations, from Google DeepMind, assimilates optical, radar, LiDAR, climate, gravimetric and even textual sources into a single time-continuous embedding field model, and emits, for each 10-meter pixel and each year, a 64-dimensional vector —quantized to 8 bits— that distills a full year of multisensor observation into a single analysis-ready code [Brown et al. 2025]. The architecture is a synthesis of everything above: a spatiotemporal encoder built on attention, trained as a multimodal autoencoder with implicit decoders that reconstruct missing modalities and dates, regularized toward a smooth and samplable latent geometry —the discipline of the VAE, the mixing of the Transformer, and the distributional intuition of text embeddings, all aimed at the planet. Published as annual, global, analysis-ready layers in Google Earth Engine from 2017 onward [Brown et al. 2025; Google 2025], these embeddings allow a practitioner to replace a bespoke, label-hungry pipeline with a nearest-neighbor search or a lightweight classifier over vectors —which is, once again and now at planetary scale, exactly the promise we started with: take a set that is almost impossible to model directly and, via a process \(f\), represent it as a well known, computable and exhaustively studied mathematical object.

title: Earth Embeddings
text:
It is not hard to define what embeddings are; the hard part is understanding how to create an embedding and how to benchmark which ones are actually useful or informative for the entities or fields they intend to represent.
Def (Embedding): In the context of mathematics and machine learning, we define an embedding \(x_i \in X\) of the object \(i \subset A\) as a vector representation of the object \(i\) where \(X \subset \mathbb{R}^n\), defined via a relation \(f\) such that: \(f:A \rightarrow X\).
The convention is that \(x_i\) is an embedding vector representing the object \(i\) of the (finite or infinite) set \(A\), while \(X\) is the embedding base (space) representing the set \(A\) itself. In the literature, and particularly in this content, embedding will be used for both depending on context, specifying only when disambiguation is required.
Some implicit expectations about embeddings —implicit since it is the goal for an embedding to satisfy them, even though they are not necessarily met in the process of generating embeddings— are the following:

The embedding base (\(X\)) must be derived exclusively from the data universe \(A\).
To each element \(a_i\) there corresponds a unique vector \(x_i\).
The minimal spanning vector space for \(X\) must keep the meaning of \(A\) embedded in the geometry of that vector space.

title: Earth Embeddings
section: Open Data Embeddings and Embedding Families
text:
Open Data Embeddings and Embedding Families
With the explosion of applications such as ChatGPT and with the growing interest in the creation of embeddings as a standard practice in ML and Deep Learning for research and commercial purposes, particularly for word embeddings, it is important to define some important concepts:
Def (Foundation Models): foundation models are a concept that includes machine learning or statistical models, weights, or inference obtained by training an algorithm at large scale that, given its general optimization objective and its multipurpose training, can be used as a starting point to serve as input or preprocessed result for a more delimited task.
Def (Transfer Learning): It refers to any action and method by which some pre-trained, fine-tuned or optimized model or algorithm is used as a starting point for subsequent training in order to improve the performance of the model itself for the original task or for any other where the training is relevant.
Given the growing use of pre-trained models and weights to improve existing models, not only because of the trust in the entities that publish the models, but also because of the growing cost of maintaining and training the necessary infrastructure required to train such models, those entities also provide models to generate embeddings or, in order to protect intellectual property, open the data of the resulting embedding bases for researchers and practitioners to use.
That is the case of ChatGPT, Meta and Google, which are pioneers in opening such datasets for text, image or Earth satellite layers.
In particular, for Earth embeddings there are three main families of embeddings with open databases.

Clay
Clay is a community-driven, fully open-source Earth foundation model, developed with Development Seed and fiscally sponsored by the non-profit Radiant Earth. It is a Vision Transformer trained through self-supervised learning with a Masked Autoencoder, which produces semantic embeddings for any location and moment. The v1 model is a 632-million-parameter network split into a 311M MAE encoder, a 15M decoder and a frozen 304M DINOv2 “teacher”, and emits 768-dimensional embeddings; training combines a 95% reconstruction loss (MSE over masked patches) with a 5% representation loss distilled from the DINOv2 teacher, so that it simultaneously optimizes pixel reconstruction and semantic structure. Its design emphasis is flexibility: it ingests a data cube of pixel values plus metadata (time, latitude/longitude, ground sampling distance and central wavelengths), pre-trained across many sensors —Sentinel-1/2, NAIP, MODIS, Landsat-8 and others— so that it works across multiple platforms and resolutions, from drones to satellites. Code and weights are Apache-2.0, documentation is CC-BY, and the published embeddings are ODC-BY on Source Cooperative —the most permissive and fully open of the three.


IBM’s Prithvi
Built jointly by IBM Research and NASA, it is the reference geospatial foundation model with open weights. It uses a temporal Vision Transformer base architecture with 3D patch embeddings —inputs are cubes of multitemporal, multispectral images split into spatiotemporal “tubelets”— and 3D positional encoding over height, width and time, trained as a Masked Autoencoder. The first release, Prithvi-EO-1.0 (100M parameters), was pre-trained on NASA’s harmonized Landsat–Sentinel-2 archive; Prithvi-EO-2.0 scales to 300M/600M parameters with global coverage and adds temporal-location embeddings, pre-trained on 4.2 million HLS time-series samples at 30-meter resolution. Training masks approximately 75% of the input patches and reconstructs them under an MSE loss. The weights are openly published on Hugging Face (ibm-nasa-geospatial) and are fine-tuned for flood mapping, wildfire scar and crop segmentation, and cloud-gap imputation [Jakubik et al. 2023, arXiv:2310.18660; Szwarcman et al. 2024, arXiv:2412.02732].


Google DeepMind’s AlphaEarth
AlphaEarth, from Google DeepMind, is the most aggressively engineered of the three and takes a different approach —an embedding field model rather than an image-crop encoder. Its Space-Time Precision encoder combines spatial and temporal attention with convolutions, and is trained as a multimodal autoencoder with implicit decoders that reconstruct missing observations across time and modalities, regularized through teacher-student consistency and contrastive alignment. It assimilates an unusually broad set of sources —optical and thermal imagery from Sentinel-2 and Landsat, cloud-penetrating radar, LiDAR-derived 3D surface measurements, elevation, climate, gravitational fields and even descriptive text. The output is a 64-dimensional embedding for each 10-meter pixel, packing a year of multi-source data into each vector, and the 32-bit embeddings are quantized to 8 bits for a 4× storage reduction with negligible performance loss. These are distributed as annual, global, analysis-ready layers (from 2017 onward, dataset version 1.1 as of November 2025) in the Google Earth Engine catalog under CC-BY 4.0 [Brown et al. 2025, arXiv:2507.22291] —open data, although the model weights themselves are not public.

title: Introduction
text:
This series of pages is an exercise carried out to assess the ability to use Earth Embeddings (vector bases) to model complex phenomena related to spatial features. This work is even more ambitious and takes it one step further by using them in an application in the field of the social sciences: crime incidents.
The intent of the book is to be a self-contained data analysis exercise for using and replicating or improving the current models and training. Thus, the referenced repository contains the scripts needed (both Python and Google Earth Engine) to replicate the analysis by following the given instructions and the pages of this book themselves. At the same time, the pages also aim to be self-contained in terms of content, where a minimal background in machine learning models, applied statistics and programming is needed to understand the present pipelines, including a basic description of geospatial concepts and techniques so the logic of the analysis can be followed based on current practice.
Finally, the repository includes data to deploy 2 small web applications to perform an EDA analysis and a demonstration of the predicted street features based on the analysis.
Thus, anyone with a general background can understand both the content as a stakeholder report and the source code to replicate and use the databases. The logic of the notes is as follows:

Understand what an embedding is.
How embeddings are typically used as features.
Data processing, modeling and training decisions.
Conclusion.

In addition, there are 3 appendices with the following purposes:

Briefly explain the algorithms, the metric evaluation and the mathematics behind the algorithms used.
Describe particular methods or logics used in the code that require explanation.
Explain the basic geospatial analysis and the operations needed to understand the decisions behind each analysis.

Furthermore, the repository itself contains an FAQ section in its README.md file.

This work is even more ambitious and takes it one step further by using them in an application in the field of the social sciences: crime incidents.

title: Introduction
text:
Organization and Notebook Context
In general, the development of this work is carried out within the framework of the Research Internship of the Master’s in Data Science at ITAM, which, as the educational organization that promotes and sponsors this project, in its pursuit of contributing to the vision of a fairer and more prosperous society, opens the way to the open development of solutions and applications of Data Science techniques with the purpose of understanding, disseminating, studying and developing phenomena of a scientific, social, economic and cultural nature. It is in this context that the present work responds to the need to provide a starting point in the use of state-of-the-art tools and data for the understanding of social phenomena such as crime. The problem is of interest to the institution, since the purpose, beyond a model, explanation or final implementation, is to provide tools and a methodology for the development of data-based applications and strategies for organizations and entities interested in modeling the phenomenon of crime, among them:

Public Security Institutions
Government agencies in general
Human rights and public policy observers
Researchers in the field
Civil Society and
The business sector.

In a context where code development solutions seem to be within everyone’s reach and, in parallel, the gap in access to information and to advances in data science development and analysis on the part of civil society appears to be increasingly concentrated in a few institutions and bodies, it is imperative to make public and to set a precedent in closing the gap between leading, frontier models and algorithms and their application to research and to the understanding of phenomena that impact society and communities. It is therefore intended that the present work be a starting point in the conversation toward the development of data-based social research within the ITAM community and, in general, for practitioners and researchers.

title: Introducción
text:
La presente serie de páginas es un ejercicio realizado para evaluar la capacidad de usar Earth Embeddings (bases vectoriales) para modelar fenómenos complejos relacionados con características espaciales. El presente trabajo es incluso más ambicioso y lleva esto un paso más allá al usarlos en una aplicación en el campo de las ciencias sociales: los incidentes delictivos.
La intención del libro es ser un ejercicio de análisis de datos autocontenido para usar y replicar o mejorar los modelos y el entrenamiento actuales. Así, en el repositorio referenciado se pueden encontrar los scripts necesarios (tanto de Python como de Google Earth Engine) para replicar el análisis siguiendo las instrucciones dadas y las propias páginas de este libro. Al mismo tiempo, las páginas pretenden ser también autocontenidas en cuanto a contenido, donde se necesita una base mínima de modelos de machine learning, estadística aplicada y programación para entender los presentes pipelines, incluyendo una descripción básica de conceptos y técnicas geoespaciales para poder seguir la lógica del análisis basada en las prácticas actuales.
Finalmente, el repositorio incluye datos para desplegar 2 pequeñas aplicaciones web para realizar un análisis EDA y una demostración de las características predichas de las calles con base en el análisis.
Así, cualquier persona con una base general puede entender tanto el contenido como un reporte para stakeholders y también el código fuente para replicar y usar las bases de datos. La lógica de las notas es la siguiente:

Entender qué es un embedding.
Cómo se usan típicamente los embeddings como características (features).
Decisiones de procesamiento de datos, modelado y entrenamiento.
Conclusión.

Además, hay 3 apéndices con los siguientes propósitos:

Explicar brevemente los algoritmos, la evaluación de métricas y las matemáticas detrás de los algoritmos usados.
Describir métodos o lógicas particulares usadas en el código que requieren explicación.
Explicar el análisis geoespacial básico y las operaciones necesarias para entender las decisiones detrás de cada análisis.

Además, el propio repositorio contiene una sección de FAQs en su archivo README.md.

title: Introducción
section: Contexto de la Organización y el Cuaderno
text:
Contexto de la Organización y el Cuaderno
En general, el desarrollo del presente trabajo se realiza dentro del marco de desarrollo de la Estancia de Investigación de la Maestría en Ciencia de Datos del ITAM, la cual, como organización educativa promotora y patrocinadora de este proyecto, en su búsqueda por aportar a la visión de una sociedad más justa y próspera, da apertura al desarrollo abierto de soluciones y aplicaciones de técnicas de Ciencia de Datos con la finalidad de entender, divulgar, estudiar y desarrollar fenómenos de carácter científico, social, económico y cultural. Es en este contexto que el presente trabajo responde a la necesidad de proporcionar un punto de partida en el uso de herramientas y datos de vanguardia para el entendimiento de fenómenos sociales como el crimen. El problema es de interés para la institución, pues la finalidad, más allá de un modelo, explicación o implementación final, se busca dar herramientas y una metodología para el desarrollo de aplicaciones y estrategias basadas en datos para organizaciones y entidades a las que sea de interés modelar el fenómeno del crimen, entre ellas están:

Instituciones de Seguridad Pública
Agencias gubernamentales en general
Observadores de derechos humanos y políticas públicas
Investigadores en la materia
Sociedad Civil y
Sector empresarial.

En un contexto donde las soluciones de desarrollo de código parecen al alcance de todos, y de manera paralela, la brecha en el acceso a la información y a los avances en materia de desarrollo en ciencia de datos y análisis por parte de la sociedad civil pareciera ser cada vez más concentrada en pocas instituciones y organismos, es imperante hacer público y sentar un precedente en cerrar la brecha entre los modelos y algoritmos punteros y en la frontera y su aplicación al uso en la investigación y el entendimiento de fenómenos que impactan a la sociedad y a las comunidades. Es entonces que se pretende con el presente trabajo un punto de partida en la conversación al desarrollo de investigación social basada en datos dentro de la comunidad ITAM y, en general, a practicantes e investigadores.

title: Embeddings de la Tierra
text:
No es difícil definir qué son los embeddings; lo difícil es entender cómo crear un embedding y cómo evaluar (benchmark) cuáles son realmente útiles o informativos para las entidades o campos que pretenden representar.
Def (Embedding): En el contexto de las matemáticas y el machine learning, definimos un embedding \(x_i \in X\) del objeto \(i \subset A\), como una representación vectorial del objeto \(i\) donde \(X \subset \mathbb{R}^n\), definida vía una relación \(f\) tal que: \(f:A \rightarrow X\).
La convención es que \(x_i\) es un vector embedding que representa al objeto \(i\) del conjunto (finito o infinito) \(A\), mientras que \(X\) es la base (espacio) de embeddings que representa al propio conjunto \(A\). En la literatura, y particularmente en este contenido, embedding se usará para ambos según el contexto, especificando solo si se requiere desambiguar.
Algunas expectativas implícitas sobre los embeddings —implícitas ya que es el objetivo que un embedding las satisfaga, aunque en el proceso de generar embeddings no necesariamente se cumplan— son las siguientes: - La base de embeddings (\(X\)) debe derivarse exclusivamente del universo de datos \(A\). - Para cada elemento \(a_i\) corresponde un único vector \(x_i\). - El espacio vectorial de expansión mínima para \(X\) debe mantener el significado de \(A\) embebido en la geometría de dicho espacio vectorial.


La necesidad de embeddings surge naturalmente en la práctica del machine learning y el modelado estadístico. Al trabajar con conjuntos de datos tabulares, hay instancias en las que, para entender y modelar fenómenos, usamos ingeniería de características, creando una serie de métricas derivadas. Otras veces el objeto que estudiamos es realmente difícil de manejar, por ejemplo texto, imágenes u objetos físicos, esto debido a sus cantidades y combinaciones de objetos finitas pero casi inmanejables, o por su comportamiento continuo y complejo; entonces crear modelos de la realidad que representan esos objetos es difícil. Para esos casos existe la opción de crear embeddings, es decir, tomar algún conjunto y, vía un proceso \(f\), algunos de los cuales se comentarán más abajo, representarlo en forma vectorial, un objeto matemático muy bien conocido, computable y estudiado.
La siguiente figura describe el proceso general para la generación de bases de embeddings, donde el modelo puede ir desde reglas de asignación simples, funciones hash o ingeniería de características, hasta salidas de redes neuronales complejas o pesos entre capas.



Proceso de generación de embeddings


Para una explicación más visual de lo que esperamos de un (buen) embedding, veamos la siguiente figura. A la izquierda tenemos la existencia de dimensiones de embedding, en las que esperamos ver que las palabras se agrupen entre sí con base en su significado semántico. Eso se traduce en un sentido geométrico, en el que objetos similares (en este ejemplo, texto) mantienen un sentido de similitud geométrica: objetos similares se envían a embeddings similares.



Caracterización ilustrativa de vectores de embedding.





Siguiendo la lógica ya esbozada, el texto es quizás el objeto canónico que se resiste al modelado ingenuo. Un corpus es un conjunto discreto cuyos átomos —palabras, subpalabras, oraciones— tienen un inventario finito, pero se combinan en un espacio de posibilidades efectivamente ilimitado; y, peor aún, el significado que nos importa no vive en los símbolos mismos sino en la compañía que mantienen. Esta es la vieja intuición distribucional, aislada por Harris y formulada de manera memorable por Firth: una palabra se caracteriza por las palabras que la rodean [Harris 1954; Firth 1957]. Un embedding de texto es entonces un mapeo
\[f : V \to \mathbb{R}^{d} \]
sobre el vocabulario de tokens \(V\) (o \(f:\Sigma^{*} \to \mathbb{R}^{d}\) sobre spans) que convierte estos objetos puramente relacionales y combinatorios en vectores sobre los cuales la geometría se vuelve semántica —la proximidad coseno aproximando el grado de relación y, célebremente, las traslaciones vectoriales aproximando analogías—. La primera generación aprendía un único vector estático por palabra a partir de estadísticas de co-ocurrencia: word2vec optimiza un objetivo autosupervisado —predecir el contexto a partir de la palabra central, o al revés— cuyo óptimo coloca cerca a las palabras con distribuciones similares [Mikolov et al. 2013], mientras que GloVe alcanza una geometría comparable factorizando una matriz global de co-ocurrencia [Pennington et al. 2014]. Sin embargo, dicha \(f\) estática no puede separar los dos sentidos de bank (banco/orilla). La segunda generación, por lo tanto, hizo contextual el embedding, dejando que \(f\) dependa de la oración completa, de modo que un mismo token recibe vectores distintos en contextos distintos —el movimiento industrializado por BERT [Devlin et al. 2019] y extendido a pasajes completos, para recuperación y clustering, por codificadores a nivel de oración como Sentence-BERT [Reimers & Gurevych 2019]. La ganancia es exactamente la prometida en el caso general: un objeto relacional intratable se reemplaza por puntos en un espacio bien conocido, computable y exhaustivamente estudiado.



Los ejemplos anteriores toman el embedding como el producto final; el autoencoder variacional vale la pena estudiarlo porque invierte el énfasis y trata el embedding como una causa latente. Supongamos que postulamos que cada dato observado \(x\) se genera a partir de un código no observado \(z\), extraído de un prior simple \(p(z)\) —convencionalmente una Gaussiana estándar— y transformado a través de un decodificador \(p_{\theta}(x \mid z)\). Embeber \(x\) ahora consiste en inferir su posterior \(p(z \mid x)\), la distribución sobre códigos que podrían haberlo producido; pero este posterior es intratable para cualquier decodificador interesante. La resolución de Kingma y Welling es aproximarlo con un codificador \(q_{\phi}(z \mid x)\) y entrenar codificador y decodificador conjuntamente maximizando la cota inferior de la evidencia (ELBO) [Kingma & Welling 2014; Rezende et al. 2014]:
\[ \log p_{\theta}(x) \ge \mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;x) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z\mid x)}\!\left[\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z)\right]}_{\text{reconstrucción}} - \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\!\left(q_{\phi}(z\mid x)\,\Vert\,p(z)\right)}_{\text{regularización}}. \]
Los dos términos se leen como una instrucción y una disciplina: reconstruir \(x\) fielmente, pero mantener la distribución del código cerca del prior, de modo que el espacio latente permanezca suave y muestreable en lugar de degenerar en una tabla de búsqueda. El único obstáculo técnico —que debemos retropropagar a través de un paso de muestreo— se elimina con el truco de reparametrización, escribiendo \(z = \mu_{\phi}(x) + \sigma_{\phi}(x)\odot\varepsilon\) con \(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\), lo que empuja la aleatoriedad hacia una variable independiente de la entrada y restaura un camino diferenciable. Lo que obtenemos, entonces, no es meramente un vector por objeto, sino un espacio de embeddings dotado de una gramática probabilística: una variedad continua y de baja dimensión a lo largo de la cual podemos interpolar y de la cual podemos muestrear —el mismo objetivo vectorial bien comportado de antes, ahora equipado con una explicación generativa de cómo surgieron los objetos.



Marco general de un VAE (Por EugenioTL - Trabajo propio, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=107231101)





Si el VAE aporta una razón probabilística para querer buenos embeddings, el Transformer aporta el mecanismo que calcula los mejores que tenemos actualmente. Su punto de partida es, una vez más, una limitación de las herramientas anteriores: los codificadores recurrentes y convolucionales construyen el contexto de forma local y secuencial, de modo que las dependencias entre elementos distantes se median a través de cadenas largas y, por consiguiente, resultan costosas de aprender. El Transformer descarta la recurrencia y permite que cada elemento atienda directamente a todos los demás mediante self-attention [Vaswani et al. 2017]. Concretamente, a partir de una matriz de entrada \(X\) se forman queries, keys y values mediante mapeos lineales, \(Q = X W_{Q}\), \(K = X W_{K}\), \(V = X W_{V}\), y se mezclan mediante \[ \mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V)\;=\;\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right) V , \] de modo que cada vector de salida es un promedio ponderado, dependiente de los datos, de todos los demás —una recuperación direccionada por contenido en la que los pesos son similitudes aprendidas y el factor \(\sqrt{d_{k}}\) simplemente mantiene los logits en una escala adecuada. Varios de estos mapeos corren en paralelo (atención multi-cabeza) para capturar distintos patrones relacionales a la vez; y dado que la operación es equivariante a permutaciones, el orden debe reinyectarse mediante codificaciones posicionales. El resultado es precisamente una máquina para el embedding contextual: consume un conjunto (o secuencia) de vectores y devuelve un conjunto de la misma forma en el que cada uno ha sido reescrito en términos de sus vecinos relevantes. Por esto la arquitectura sustenta los embeddings de texto contextuales anteriores; por esto —con las imágenes cortadas en parches y tratadas como tokens— da lugar al Vision Transformer [Dosovitskiy et al. 2021]; y por esto, combinada con un objetivo de reconstrucción enmascarada al estilo del autoencoder enmascarado [He et al. 2022], se ha convertido en el motor por defecto para aprender representaciones de casi cualquier objeto que podamos serializar en tokens.



Arquitectura base de un Vision Transformer (Por Davide Coccomini - Trabajo propio, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=110678226)





Lo cual nos lleva al objeto más difícil de la lista. La superficie de la Tierra no es ni un vocabulario finito ni una imagen ordenada; es un campo continuo y tetradimensional, observado solo indirectamente, a través de una flota heterogénea de instrumentos. A veces la vemos en bandas ópticas y térmicas (Sentinel-2, Landsat); otras veces mediante radar que penetra las nubes (Sentinel-1 SAR), altimetría láser de la estructura de la vegetación (GEDI, LiDAR), variables climáticas de reanálisis (ERA5-Land), o incluso el campo gravitacional del planeta (GRACE) —cada una con su propia resolución, cadencia y régimen de ruido, y cada una plagada de vacíos dejados por nubes, órbita y tiempo de revisita—. La dificultad de modelado es entonces de un tipo distinto al del texto: no la combinatoria de un conjunto discreto, sino la fusión de muchas vistas parciales, continuas y mal registradas de un sistema en evolución —agravada por la escasez que domina el campo, a saber, petabytes de píxeles contra muy pocas etiquetas, porque un solo dato de verdad-de-campo (ground truth) significa que alguien visitó físicamente un lugar en un momento dado [Jakubik et al. 2023; Brown et al. 2025]. La respuesta natural ha sido importar en bloque la maquinaria recién descrita: tratar pilas de imágenes satelitales como cubos de tokens espacio-temporales, preentrenar un codificador Vision-Transformer mediante reconstrucción enmascarada, y así aprender una representación general de la superficie sin etiquetas —la estrategia de los modelos fundacionales geoespaciales como Prithvi, preentrenado de forma autosupervisada en el archivo armonizado Landsat–Sentinel y luego ajustado para mapeo de inundaciones, segmentación de cultivos y similares [Jakubik et al. 2023; Szwarcman et al. 2024]. El objeto es monstruoso, pero la receta es la conocida: encontrar un mapeo \(f\) hacia un espacio vectorial computable.
La culminación es llevar la idea del embedding a su extremo literal y vectorizar el planeta mismo: asignar a cada lugar, y a cada año, un código compacto que resuma todo lo que los instrumentos, en conjunto, dicen sobre él. Han surgido dos lecturas complementarias de “embedding de la Tierra”. En la primera, se embebe la ubicación: SatCLIP aprende un codificador de ubicación alineando de forma contrastiva coordenadas geográficas —elevadas a la esfera mediante características posicionales de armónicos esféricos— con la imaginería satelital observada en ese lugar, produciendo un \(f : (\mathrm{lat}, \mathrm{lon}) \to \mathbb{R}^{d}\) ligero cuyos vectores ya predicen temperatura, densidad poblacional o presencia de especies en un punto [Klemmer et al. 2025]. En la segunda lectura, más abarcadora, se embebe directamente el campo de la superficie: AlphaEarth Foundations, de Google DeepMind, asimila fuentes ópticas, de radar, LiDAR, climáticas, gravimétricas e incluso textuales en un único modelo de campo de embeddings continuo en el tiempo, y emite, para cada píxel de 10 metros y cada año, un vector de 64 dimensiones —cuantizado a 8 bits— que destila un año completo de observación multisensor en un único código listo para análisis [Brown et al. 2025]. La arquitectura es una síntesis de todo lo anterior: un codificador espacio-temporal construido sobre atención, entrenado como un autoencoder multimodal con decodificadores implícitos que reconstruyen modalidades y fechas faltantes, regularizado hacia una geometría latente suave y muestreable —la disciplina del VAE, la mezcla del Transformer, y la intuición distribucional de los embeddings de texto, todo apuntado hacia el planeta—. Publicadas como capas anuales, globales y listas para análisis en Google Earth Engine desde 2017 en adelante [Brown et al. 2025; Google 2025], estos embeddings permiten a un practicante reemplazar un pipeline a medida y hambriento de etiquetas por una búsqueda de vecinos más cercanos o un clasificador ligero sobre vectores —lo cual es, una vez más y ahora a escala planetaria, exactamente la promesa con la que comenzamos: tomar un conjunto casi imposible de modelar directamente y, vía un proceso \(f\), representarlo como un objeto matemático bien conocido, computable y exhaustivamente estudiado.
